subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to adequately protect the Canadian environment from toxic and hazardous waste and for its subservience to the vested interests of the chemical and industrial waste producers and, in particular, for its failure to expedite the clean-up of the Great Lakes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak this morning, and particularly to move the motion condemning the Government for its subservience to big industry. I am going to spend my time this morning dealing with the two major sides of the issue, one being the serious problem of no proper toxic and hazardous waste handling sites in Canada and the lack of law at both the provincial and federal levels; and also, in relation to the United States, the very serious problem we have encountered, not only under the present administration of Mr. Reagan but, in terms of the last 40 years, what has been happening to the Great Lakes and the water supply which provides water for four million Canadians and most of the 48 States in the U.S.
It appears, Mr. Speaker, through the documentation I am going to put on the record today, that there is really a conspiracy of inaction on both sides of the border to turn the entire Great Lakes system into a dump. The reason I say that is that very few Canadians know, and very few Hon. Members of this House seem to know, that the water which is now flowing out of the St. Lawrence River came down as rainfall and ran into the Great Lakes at about the same time as Columbus came to North America. It takes about 500 years for the water to recirculate throughout the Great Lakes sytem and ultimately to go out into the Atlantic. What has happened over the last four years is that the big businesses, particularly the chemical industry and the war industry in the United States, have consciously chosen certain areas near the Canadian border to store improperly large amounts of toxic and hazardous waste. Perhaps the largest of those is the Niagara Escarpment where, over the past 40 years, things such as entire trains have been driven there. Big pits have been dug in the ground and they have simply driven the train right into the ground and buried it because it is contaminated with radioactivity.
Four years ago, the U.S. Government, in collusion with the U.S. Army, dumped millions of gallons of radioactive waste from the Manhattan project directly into the Niagara system, and you can still see a huge tower there if you go to Niagara Falls which is filled with radioactive waste from the Manhattan project.
Tied in with all of that are the more serious chemical dumps, such as S-site, Hyde Park, 102nd Street and the Love Canal, which have gained their great notoriety not because of the work of Government bureaucrats and politicians, but because of concerned citizens and a few concerned medical experts such as Dr. Beverley Paigen, who started to study why there were so many stillbirths, so many spontaneous abortions, why people were getting lesions, why children were going deaf, why there were personality disorders, and so on, in relation to these dumps.
Why would a large chemical company sell for $1 an area where they knew houses and schools were going to be built, knowing full well those wastes were not like old paper bags and rotten logs, but that we were talking about a long-term pollution problem which was going to cause serious damage? Where big business cannot buy politicians-here I am talking about Canadian politicians, Liberals and Conservatives, and in the United States, Democrats and Republicans-where they cannot buy them to keep them from forcing the proper cleanup either through the introduction of the law or through the introduction of a clean-up fund, the companies simply go around it.
I will give an example of this on the U.S. side and an example on the Canadian side. Under President Carter, what was known as the "super fund" was set up which taxed all of the chemical industry in the United States, rated on the amount of waste products they produced. Now there is $1 billion sitting in that fund. The money is not being spent for two reasons; one, big business has gone to Reagan and said: "Look, if you make us clean it up it is going to lower our profits. We are in a recession. You cannot make us do that. We have been getting away with it for a long time, anyway." On the other hand, if Reagan allows the super fund to be spent, he knows that part of the super fund expenditures would include the expenditure of tax dollars. Taxpayers in municipalities and States, in the United States, and federal politicians, would say: "Why are we paying for it? Why do we have to have this super fund? Why are we involved in the clean-up?" Inevitably, there would be a public outcry. There would be a fall in the stock market. At the very least, these chemical companies would start to become unpopular. Those are the two

reasons on the U.S. side why they will not spend the super fund and big business simply will not clean up.
On the Canadian side, we simply do not have proper law. It should be constitutional, but the Government refuses to accept the concept of having the environment dealt with in the Constitution. In a few moments I am going to go through some of the constitutional problems we are having now in terms of law, the correlation between federal and provincial jurisdiction, and the real lack of law and regulations to deal with these kinds of contaminants.
Knowing that we have such paltry law in Canada now, one example which I have raised many times in this House, Mr. Speaker, is Amax. In the middle of the 1979 federal election, the Liberal Government decided that that particular company, Amax, required a special dumping permit which exceeded federal guidelines by 8,000 times. The Member of Parliament at that time was a Liberal Cabinet Minister who is now the President of the Liberal Party, but the net goes much further, Mr. Speaker, The present Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario, Mr. Aird, was on the Amax international board. When he stepped down to become the Lieutenant-Governor, he was replaced by the former President of the United States, Gerald Ford. So there we have the international connection of big business. What happened after that? It is very clear Mr. Aird's firm continued to do the legal work for Amax.

speechtext:
Senator Aird, a well-known bagman for the Liberal Party. He simply went to the Cabinet and said: "Look, I need some kind of special permit for my buddies in Amax; they want to dump one million metric tons into the fishing ground". Of course,the local media for months and months said: "Oh, it is just the Nishga Indians; they are just trying to force their land claims. It has nothing to do with pollution." But then some independent scientists came on board, church groups and trade unionists got involved, and they finally managed to get rid of the former Minister of Fisheries and Oceans because I understand that some 80,000 letters ended up going to the Prime Minister's Office. I tabled in this House correspondence regarding that issue. There is real concern about such paltry law. First, we should beef it up, but even where we have, Canadians are concerned because politicians, certainly in the Liberal Party, seem to be prepared to run around the law and provide big business with whatever kind of dumping permit they want.
The problem is right across Canada, and let me deal with it from the Canadian side first. In British Columbia alone
266,000	dry tons of hazardous waste was produced last year. It was all improperly dumped. There is no safe site in British Columbia, none anywhere in Canada. Last year ten million dry tons were produced and a million of those were toxic, hazardous waste, dangerous to human life, dangerous to wildlife and to our water supply. So it is right across the country. If a Canadian, some Member of this House, decided
to poison his or her husband or wife and put the same kinds of stuff into a glass of water and fed it to their spouse day after day, under the Criminal Code in Canada they would be prosecuted and probably convicted for attempted murder. But the big companies can dump it in the Great Lakes.
On the American side, the U.S. military and big chemical companies can dump it into the water supply. Laws are diverted or changed, politicians are bought, and what is happening right now is that toxic waste is going into the Great Lakes system. By the conscious inaction of not bringing in new laws and taking the appropriate action, the decision has been made-perhaps knowingly, perhaps unwittingly-by politicians on both sides to allow 20 per cent of the fresh water supply of this planet to become polluted and turned into a septic dump.
There have been statements such as this, Mr. Speaker. Our task force met with the Vice-President of Hooker in New York State a year ago. We asked him what he was doing. The Curtin decision was coming down, and it is totally inappropriate. We are following the same route on the S-site dump, going through the court and getting improper clean-up. What does the Vice-President of Hooker have to say to concerned Canadians? He stands up, after showing us some phony movie, and says: "Well, look, Mr. Fulton, we are waiting so that we can have genetic engineering make some progress, so they can engineer some bugs. We will take containers of bugs, throw them into these toxic pits and they will eat all the problem away." The man has been living in Disneyland too long, Mr. Speaker. He drank out of a Mickey Mouse cup. It gives you some idea of the way these large corporations are prepared to deal with public concern.
Mr. David Suzuki spoke in my riding quite recently, in Kitimat, Mr. Speaker. There were a lot of young people there and he wanted to give some explanation of the concern he has for the way the Canadian parliamentary system is going. 1 think it is something all of us in this House need reflect on. The average understanding of modern science by Members of this House right now is the same as that of elementary school children. A grade seven child in Canada right now has a better understanding of science than Members of this House. We really need to get to work on that because this issue of toxic waste is no joke. It is something which is coming on us in the same way typhoid fever did at the turn of the century, which is why we got the original 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty.
At the turn of the century, 446 Canadians out of every
100,000	were dying from typhoid fever because of sewage and other kinds of pollution going into the Great Lakes. We got the Treaty and started to move on it. The United States is not attempting to live up to the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement of 1978. I do not condemn Canada in this matter because we are at least going to live up to the requirements in relation to phosphorous and so on, but there are some enormous loopholes in the Agreement and they are there by the design of the Government in office at the moment in its support of big business.
January 27, 1983

On garbage day, Mr. Speaker, would you go out of your house and throw your garbage over the fence into your neighbour's yard? You would not, for a number of reasons. There are laws against such actions and there is the law of decency. You could be prosecuted for doing it and you could go to jail. There is a law for individual Canadians, but our neighbours in the United States are dumping literally thousands of tons of this material on the Escarpment, knowing full well that for the next 40 years it will go into our water supply.
Gallup polls show that 75 per cent of Canadians support the clean-up and preservation of the Canadian environment, even if it means accepting a lower standard of living. The same Gallup polls indicate that Members of this House of Commons and members of the legislatures in the country are rated in the same category as convicted sex killers. We have to wonder about that, Mr. Speaker. Why are Canadians prepared to make that kind of economic sacrifice? It is so that they can fish with their grandchildren, so that they can drink clean water, so that they can see trees growing around them and see the odd fox running about.
Politicians will not respond, however. Each week more money is spent on cat food in the Province of Ontario than is spent by the federal Government to deal with the Great Lakes and acid rain problems in the country. More money is spent on cat food than on environmental protection, which is the greatest problem we will face in this century in this country.
Acid rain is a serious thing but the problems of dioxin, mirex and so on are a moving problem. We can deal with the courts on the U.S. side and we can clutch at straws, but we have had the Curtin decision-an utter, abject failure. The EPA tells people to go ahead and move back into the Love Canal area while nine out of eleven renowned U.S. scientists advise people not to move back into the area because the EPA studies are inaccurate and incomplete. They advise that to move back would endanger life.
The whole issue is profit maximization, Mr. Speaker. Big business says that if they have to put a prophylactic around waste, if they have to contain the waste properly and permanently and have to recycle it, their profits will go down. So they go to Ronnie in the States and say: "Ronnie, don't make us spend from the super fund, don't make us clean up; we want high profits and we want deregulation".
Deregulation on this issue means that the health of four million Canadians and one million Americans along the Great Lakes is seriously endangered. We know that one two-hundredths of a drop of dioxin will kill you where you sit, Mr. Speaker. If a beam of sunlight comes through a window and a fleck of dioxin-laden dust, weighing one ten-thousandth of a gram, floats into that sunlight, that amount can kill an entire family. In the Great Lakes region, just one-quarter ounce of dioxin could kill five million people. A ton of it is sitting in Hyde Park and they are just repumping the leachate. That is all the United States is doing. Two hundred tons of contaminated stillbottoms is sitting in S-dump, leaching into the
Supply
Niagara. It is going underwater into Canada, into Lake Ontario and contaminating the Lake.
We can study the migration patterns of that stuff coming across the Lake and we can tell that the water is becoming more and more polluted. According to the general accounting office in the United States, according to our DOE officials, according to the IJC, the Lake is becoming more and more polluted with dangerous waste.
All that is happening is a couple of frivolous little court cases. The Minister of the Environment tells us that we are employing quiet diplomacy. But stuff is moving across the Lake, Mr. Speaker, and is now being found in the tissues of dead people in this country. In that cadaver from Kingston, dioxin was found in the body tissues. The stuff is moving through the biosphere. It moves in the air, in the water, across the Lake.
The answer being given by the Liberal and Conservative Parties in this country is that the matter will be studied. When people start to get diseases and die, then they will say: "We must put in water filtration systems; we must raise municipal and other taxes". I have some answers that are going to short-circuit that and I hope the House will support me in pursuing them.
What we need is constitutional law. I am glad to see the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) here because in his constituency there are terrible problems in relation to toxic waste.
I wrote to every fire chief in Canada and had responses from most of them. The Government had never written to them nor had any other Member of Parliament. They were concerned about the waste in their communities. They do not know how to fight most of those fires. They see it going into the water supply. It is going into the Ottawa River which is not fit to swim in any more. One cannot fish in the Great Lakes. We cannot sell our eels to West Germany; they are contaminated with mirex. The situation is serious. We need proper constitutional law, and I am going to come to specific recommendations in that regard in a moment.
I am making a very serious proposal to the House today, which is to put a head tax on Americans coming into Canada. I say that in all seriousness, and I am going to explain why. Over 30 million Americans came into Canada last year, many because they have relatives here, many to fish or to hunt or as tourists. What I am saying is that if we were to charge them a head tax of $5 or $10 at the airports, at the border crossings as they came in, and we had proper information there, we could explain to them that the reason we were doing this is the toxic waste coming from Niagara, the Hanford site, and because of what is happening to our water system and our environment from acid rain. We could say: "Here is a card; what state are you from? Here is your Congressman, here is your Senator. We are charging this tax, we are raising money, because we are going to go about this in a serious way."

When 75 per cent of Canadians support reducing their standard of living to clean up, I think it is about time we sent a strong message to those Americans, our brothers and sisters from the United States, who are prepared to take a message back to the brontosaurus in the White House. That is the description used by an American who is interested in preserving the Great Lakes.
The next step is that instead of just monitoring what is happening in the Great Lakes, we have to have a proper, complete, thorough study of the costs of complete carbon filtration so we can get pure water back out of those Lakes. That is a figure this House needs to know, because we are talking billions and billions of dollars. The complacent administration of Mr. Reagan desires to be buddy-buddy with big business interests, not to protect the health of the citizens, but to protect the profit structure of big business. We need those figures so we can send the proper message.
There are a lot of council members in southern Ontario who would like to go to the their voters and say: "Look, if the federal Government does not move and get some action out of the U.S. pretty quickly on stopping this crap from going into our water system, we will have to raise the mill rates pretty drastically". For St. Catharines, we are talking about hundreds of millions of dollars for proper water filtration. For Ontario, we are talking billions. 1 think we need to get that message out.
The fourth item is that a large delegation needs to go from this Chamber, along with concerned citizens and scientists, to Congress. I am not talking about three or four, I am talking about 50 or 100 Members of this House. We need to talk about acid rain and we need to talk about toxic waste; that is the issue of this decade in terms of personal health in this country.
1 would like to put a few quotes on the record so that the Minister, when he speaks today, will have something to respond to.

We will see when I finish whether or not the Minister is going to be so eager to speak and face questions in this House. Here is an article from August, 1980 entitled: "MP angered as Ottawa backs U.S. waste pipeline". It reads:
The federal Government has conditionally supported a U.S. pipeline that would dump one million gallons of treated chemical waste a day into the Niagara River, despite the fact it cannot accurately predict the damage to nearby water supplies.
That was a concern raised by a Liberal Member. Another article was entitled: "Knew about hazards, U.S. put toxic wastes into river, report says". It is very clear that this is a letter from Union Carbide to the U.S. Army. It reads:
Plan 2 (using shallow wells) is favoured because our law department advises us it is considered impossible to determine the course of subterranean streams and, therefore, the responsibility for any contamination could not be fixed.
I have all kinds of stuff that I will be putting on the record one way or the other today, but there are a couple of quick shots that I would like to get off before I run out of time. The first is in relation to the Minister's most recent comments about the S-dump. On december 8, 1982, we find in The Gazette the following: "U.S. dump no threat to our water: Minister." Then there is a picture of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts). But what happens less than a month later? Headlines in The Globe and Mail read: "Leakage turns water into "toxic brew"." What about this headline in The Toronto Star? "Ottawa starts study of poisons in water". And in the Toronto Sun we find this headline: "5 million lives at risk".
A month ago the Minister was telling Pollution Probe that there was no problem with the dump. But suddenly the dump is the biggest issue in the country. As far as the Tories are concerned, I ran across something most interesting about them. The Tories have an environment critic but they do not allow him to ask any questions. I suppose that is because of a caucus decision not to. The only question that has been raised by the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) and the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan) in the last three years concerning the environment was whether or not to permit the importation into Canada of raccoon dogs. There is the Tory policy on the environment. At least the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) has asked a couple of questions concerning Niagara and I am grateful that he has done so; but Tory policy is to worry about raccoon dogs being imported into Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague from the New Democratic Party has painted a very bleak picture of the environmental situation in Canada. However, I am sure he has not gone to see for himself what has been done in recent years, and I think the Minister would probably be the best person to provide a list of our achievements in this area. In any case, I can assure the Hon. Member that the Members from Quebec whose ridings are located on the shores of the St. Lawrence, as mine is, are aware that eventually, the water from the Great Lakes will pass their doorstep. I must say that I am rather surprised at the Hon. Member's attitude, when he asks us to lay down the law instead of consulting with the scientific community, which, for instance, has just published reports on acid rain tending to support our Canadian theories on the subject. I think we have made progress in recent years, thanks to the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts).
Finally, the obvious question after listening to my hon. colleague's speech is: What other measures does the New Democratic Party have to recommend, besides a head tax on all Americans coming into Canada? In any case, the number of tourists has dropped, and in the final instance, international relations and our reputation as a good neighbour would suffer.
January 27, 1983

In fact, although the Hon. Member's purpose is to get at the big companies, it would be the individual citizen who would be punished and would have to pay.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the Hon. Member could inform the House how he intends to ask industry to become self-regulating. I also think he should take a look at what has already been done. In my riding, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of chemical industries and all the oil refineries that have invested millions of dollars in recent years. Furthermore, we must not forget that this is a joint responsibility. The Hon. Member tends to overlook the fact that provinces and municipalities also have a role to play here, and that citizens should insist on their discharging those responsibilities. Instead of listening to all this gloom and doom, I would rather hear some specific solutions to the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the Hon. Member's question. I would have hoped the Hon. Member for Montreal-Mercier (Mrs. Hervieux-Payette) would have listened to the recommendations I made which were to deal with the issue. The whole issue of constitutional law is something that has to be looked at very carefully.
Let me quote briefly to the Hon. Member from a report to Congress by the Controller-General in relation to the Great Lakes. I am sure the Hon. Member knows that the biological symptoms are there now for all to see. In the St. Lawrence the local population of whales is now biologically sterile as a result of the effluent that is entering the St. Lawrence from the Great Lakes. We should not forget, as I said earlier, that the water coming down as rainfall and entering the Great Lakes takes 500 years to circulate and to exit into the St. Lawrence. It takes a long time for the Great-Lakes to clean themselves. I am not just talking about a head tax alone, but that is one of the ways to mobilize our friends and neighbours to the south of us so as to get to the politicians who have been bought by big industry.
Let us be very clear about this. Big business has said very clearly that it will not clean up its dumps. Big business will not put a prophylactic around its waste, nor will big business recycle waste. President Reagan will not spend money from the super fund. He will not clean up. We are now taking the worst of ail alternatives, which is to allow the courts in the United States to come up with completely inappropriate resolutions.
Here is what the Controller-General in the United States had to say about this issue:
As early as 1970 EPA and IJC recognized that toxic pollution is potentially a greater threat to the Great Lakes than eutrophication. Toxic pollution could endanger human health, destroy Great Lakes commercial fishing, and ultimately render the lakes useless for a variety of desirable activities.
In fiscal year 1981, the IJC Toxic Substances Committee reported that more than 30,000 chemical compounds were produced in the Great Lakes Basin. To date, over 450 of the
Supply
chemical compounds have been found in the Lake. Here is what the EPA has to say about what they will do:
EPA generally concurs with our discussion of toxics, except for three points. First, EPA cites that some evidence indicates that controls over toxic pollutants can be effective.
That is a great statement.
Second, EPA points out that the Food and Drug Administration sets allowable limits of toxic levels in fish.
That is interesting, since the EPA itself, before Reagan came into office, said that there should be no dioxin level allowed in drinking water. None whatsoever. The third point:
And finally, EPA believes that the issue of laboratory capacity and capability is not an issue peculiar to the Great Lakes.
EPA has a three-year backlog on fish samples which have been taken from the Great Lakes which have not been tested because they say they do not have the lab capacity.
We are dealing with an administration that will not deal with the issue on both sides of the Canadian-U.S. border. I suggest that we need to go to Congress with a major group to look at some kind of a head tax and to educate our American friends who are coming here that we are being seriously damaged in terms of health, recreation and tourism by their actions on acid rain and toxic waste.
We need to take action with law. The toxic and hazardous waste Bill was passed in July, 1980, and we still have not been presented with regulations for the first third. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) says that it will be up to five years before we receive that and constitutional legal experts in Canada say that those regulations will simply not be able to deal with this issue of toxic and hazardous wastes.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) would not want to mislead the House. While I appreciate many of the remarks which he made this morning, his first remark-he can correct me if I am wrong- indicated that we could not fish in the Great Lakes or eat fish from the Great Lakes. Swimming is available at beautiful beaches and there is sport fishing. The Hon. Member's statement that we cannot eat the fish from the Great Lakes is not true. Mr. Speaker, with regard to the first question concerning fish, I think if the Hon. Member checks Hansard he will see that I was thinking about certain areas of the Great Lakes that are now permanently closed to the commercial fisheries because of high levels of PCBs and dioxin. There are also some other areas closed simply because of localized pollution.
I would like to quote from Dr. Beverley Paigen to indicate why I say the problems in relation to the fishery in the Great Lakes are becoming serious. Dr. Paigen is a renowned scientist in the United States in relation to Great Lakes pollution problems. The task force document states:
Paigen stated that Lake Ontario has been tremendously affected by toxic chemicals in the Niagara River. 'I don't feel that these (Lake Ontario) fish are fit for human consumption,' the scientist famous for her involvement in the Love Canal said. 'I would not eat the fish.'
We are not talking about all of the fish or all of the species in the Great Lakes, but our eel populations have been banned from sale in West Germany because of the high levels of mirex. Commercial fisheries, particularly trout and some other species in various localized areas of the Great Lakes, are now closed for export and catchment. There are areas where they can be caught but there is an interesting juggle in this area.

Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious subject, but I do not think the motion which has been presented to us is very serious. The subject which underlies it is. 1 would like to take at least a few moments to put on the record what has been done, not only over the past year but a little bit before that as well. It was not in any way given reference by the hon. gentleman who moved the motion, either because he was not aware of what had been done or perhaps, more probably because it would not support the rather distorted motion which he has presented to the House.
Just in terms of this Parliament, a variety of actions have been taken within a larger context. Just to note a few of them specifically, there has been the passing of the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act. The Hon. Member referred to it and indicated that he thought the regulations would not be brought forward for another "four or five years", I believe that was the phrase he used. That is simply not true. Some of the regulations have been gazetted. They have been undertaken after an extensive process of publication. The rest are expected to be presented very soon.
There has been the signature in July, 1982 of something like $65 million worth of expenditure from Canada, in conjunction with the Province of Ontario, directed to the further clean-up of the Great lakes water systems, particularly through the support of sewage facilities.
There have been very strong efforts, led by Canada, at the international level. Environment Canada chaired committees of the OECD directed to bringing into line, into some coherence, the international assessment, treatment and study of the production of chemicals. There has been a complete attempt to develop an international system for rating, providing, if you like, a passport for chemicals as they are developed so that, internationally, we can co-operate and co-ordinate our efforts to control the hazards of toxic chemicals.
There has been no awareness on the part of the Hon. Member that over the past three years, through cost-sharing agreements with the Provinces, we have financed extensive studies to detect existing hazardous dump sites and also to bring forward the information and plans needed to provide a network of clean-up facilities in order to remove and destroy existing hazardous sites and also to deal with the coming on to the market of toxic, hazardous goods.
There has been no indication that the Hon. Member understands that the federal Government, in co-operation with the Provinces, has offered to provide Crown land, if it should be
Supply
requested, in order to provide needed disposal sites in this country.
There has been no recognition that considerable research is being done in these areas, that something over $75 million a year is being expended by the federal Government on research into toxic areas.
There has been no indication that the Hon. Member even realizes that the Toxic Chemicals Management Program has been established within the federal Government. It was established in 1980 and is designed to provide a "cradle-to-the-grave" management approach to the handling of toxic chemicals, not only to prevent newly-produced toxic compounds from entering the environment, but also to clean up, to remove, those which are known to be present. The program provides a focus for all of Environment Canada's toxic chemical-related activities. We are expanding and developing the program and, in conjunction with the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers, we are assessing priorities at the national and regional levels.
The Toxic Chemicals Management Program includes measurement to ascertain concentrations present in the environment, inventories-that is, an assessment of the quantities and point sources of toxic releases-and characteristics research, for instance, impacts on wildlife toxicity, bioaccumulation and persistence.
We are concentrating our work on four essential areas of concern: pesticides, radionuclides, new chemicals and existing chemicals. Part of this work is being done in other departments, of course. For instance, pesticide evaluation is undertaken by Agriculture Canada. The examination of radionuclides is being rearranged to provide new policy direction within the Department of the Environment, and the study of new chemicals is being considered internationally with respect to manufacturers' pre-marketing data to provide adequate protection against potentially harmful chemicals.
In his speech, the Hon. Member gave no sign of recognition that he is even aware that these developments-which are known, I think, to most Hon. Members of the House-have been taking place.
The resolution which the New Democratic Party has presented focuses largely on the Great Lakes. Therefore, let us consider what has been happening in that area. Since the signing of the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement in 1972, which will come to the end of its next phase by 1985, $1.3 billion will have been spent on the upgrading of sewage plant systems in Ontario, exactly because of the past impact they have had on the Great Lakes.
There has been the passing of the phosphorous limitation regulations in 1970 and 1973. The Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) in speaking about Lake Erie, correctly pointed out that, as a result of these phosphorous regulations, the quality of the water in Lake Erie has been enormously strengthened and the fisheries have been returning to prosperity.

An important part of what we must do is to spur the United States on to greater and faster action, and that we have been doing. speechtext: So you could ignore them.

speechtext:
-United States court and regulatory process. We are not bringing presentations through the American court and regulatory systems. We are not doing that because we believe that that effort on the part of the federal Government would likely be counter-productive. If we attempted to use the American court system to resolve these problems, it is quite likely that the American administration would say: "If you have chosen to use the court system, you must live with it. It is a lengthy and expensive process and you must abide by its results. Do not come to us to respond to your problems; you, have gone to the courts to deal with them." We believe that that would be counterproductive.
We believe that through direct negotiations with the United States, we can impress upon them their obligations to us, which are not necessarily legal obligations, but, rather, are moral and political obligations of a good neighbour to another. Therefore, we have not chosen the court process, not because we are opposed in principle to doing so, but, rather, because we
do not think that that is the best way to promote Canadian interest.
However, we have been anxious to support others who use the American court process, such as the special interest groups which have standing before the American court process. We have opened up our advice, expertise and knowledge to them and they have expressed their thanks for what we are doing.
It is fair enough to ask, if those are the methods we are using, is there any reason to believe that they are succeeding? Indeed, there is some evidence to that effect. I believe it is because of the kinds of interventions that we have made with the United States authorities that, for instance, the American administration has responded to the problem involving the Niagara Falls, New York sewage treatment plant, which is the major polluter of the Niagara region. I think it was as a result of interventions on our part that the permit was issued in November, 1982 to proceed with that project and the funds to support it were unblocked in Washington.
At one stage the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) referred to something which was a bit garbled. I was not quite sure what he was referring to when he spoke in support of a pipeline development; I think he was referring to the SCA issue in the Niagara Peninsula. It was as a result of our interventions with the American authorities, both the United States Government and the State of New York, that the SCA waste facility permit was tightened. It was made to conform with those guidelines which should be met. That is a result of our efforts. We have been monitoring the situation. We know that the effluent which has been coming from the SCA facility, certainly up to this point, does have a risk point which seems to meet adequate standards.
It is because of action on our part that we brought forward the two comprehensive base line reports in 1980 and 1981. It is because of our work that we were able to bring forward the Canadian Niagara River Program in August, 1982. I hope the Hon. Member has had a look at it. It was not clear from his remarks whether he has. It was partially as a result of technical assistance which we provided to environmental groups that improvements in court orders in the United States have taken place. I am not arguing that all of the court orders are completely satisfactory from our point of view, certainly they are not but they are an improvement over what would have happened otherwise.
I have already mentioned the support we gave to interested groups, the creation of the Niagara River Toxics Committee and the bilateral consultation committee of senior officials. What has been the effect of those bilateral consultations? I can cite some examples of what they have done. Funds for the Niagara Falls sewage treatment plant were allocated. There has been increased funding on the part of New York State for responding to Niagara problems. We have provided much improved controls through the Niagara River Toxics Committee.
January 27, 1983

The United States Environmental Protection Agency brought forward a Niagara frontier agenda which was a clearer response to problems than existed before. The United States has rewritten 25 major industrial discharge permits to take into account the kinds of concerns that Canadians have been expressing. There has been a speeding up of hazardous waste landfill site litigation in the United States. The United States K Corps of Engineers has been investing much more money into the study of dump site impact on groundwater quality.
I am not arguing that this is the best of all possible worlds. I am not arguing that there is still not a lot to be done. What I am arguing is that there is evidence that the impact of our interventions with the United States is having a favourable effect.
If we are acting on the situation, why is the situation becoming worse, and why did we not act before? The answer is that the situation is not getting worse. As we have already mentioned, there has been a decline in the phosphorous levels in Lake Erie. There has been a decline, since its detection, of mirex in the Great Lakes by a ten-fold span. The same is true of PCBs, DDT and dioxin. Over the past eight, nine or ten years in each case there has been roughly a ten-fold decline in the levels which have been found in the Great Lakes.
It is not that the situation is not improved. It is improving but needs to improve even further. The quality of water in the Great Lakes is improving. What is really happening is that our mechanisms of scientific detection have become so sophisticated in relation to these problems that we face an information explosion. We are now able to detect very minute quantities of a whole range of substances not previously detected in the Great Lakes water. Our knowledge is growing exponentially. As it grows, we act. However, we cannot act until we know what situations we face. One of the real problems is that we are now able to detect such minute quantities that we have the capacity to frighten people if we are careless and irresponsible, as I think the Hon. Member for Skeena has been in discussing these issues; we are able to frighten people in some circumstances without being able to give them iron-clad assurances of the significance of what we are finding.
To try and put it graphically, we know that chlorine is a tremendous poison, yet small quantities are put without hazard into swimming pools. It is poisonous, yet at a certain level it is not only satisfactory but is perhaps conducive to health. One could say that salt is made up of two terrible poisons, sodium and chlorine, yet in that combination they are harmless.
What we are able to do now with our scientific techniques is to indicate the presence in such small quantities of many substances which are normally thought of as poisonous without being able to say that at that level they constitute any hazard. There are really serious problems which are posed to us in the situation we now have. There are real problems of how we manage and act, given the information explosion that is occurring in toxic chemicals, how we manage the assessment of what we are finding and how we establish priorities for looking at them.
Supply
I can say to all Members of this House that an ordinary cup of coffee contains hundreds of substances. The aroma of a cup of coffee contains something like a dozen substances which could be considered to be toxic, yet we are not able to assess the significance of finding those toxic substances in such small amounts. If we multiply that example by others, when we have this extraordinary range of information, to say nothing of the synergistic effects of the combination of these chemicals, how are we to manage their assessment? How are we to both inform and educate the public at the same time?
The second very serious problem we have is how to bring into line the evolution of our approach to environmental matters, with proper public assessment of them. Originally, ten years ago, the general approach to pollution problems, that we took was roughly that which is still used in a rather emotional way by the Hon. Member for Skeena. That is, the policeman approach-stop whatever is happening; find out what is happening and stop it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: The honest cop.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Yes, the policeman's role, the honest policeman's role. There is nothing dishonest about saying there are hazards out there, let us find out about them and stop them. But we have moved beyond the simple policeman's role, the honest cop role to a somewhat more sophisticated approach of attempting to develop preventive pollution measures; not simply to find out what has happened and stop and correct it, but to try and act in order to prevent such situations recurring.
As we have done that more and more, we have found that we move into different areas of planning and managing levels of risk in relation to these situations. We can never assure people that everything they deal with will be absolutely safe, but we have to manage the advantages and disadvantages of the situation. We have the problem of not being able to give people 100 per cent assurance. We have the problem of trying to persuade them that there are better ways of managing our affairs so as to minimize risk.
It is a problem which is reflected in a particularly acute form in the NIMBY syndrome; that is, "Not in my back yard; we do not want anti-pollution clean-up plants close to us because there is some risk". No scientist will ever be able to assure you that there is absolutely no risk. There has to be an acceptance of risk in some areas if there is to be markedly less risk in the general treatment in society.
Those are serious matters. They are ones I would like to see Members more involved with in this House than they have yet been. I would like to see Members from all Parties asking for more briefing and information. Remarkably little of that comes to us.
There has been tremendous progress in relation to environmental protection. A great deal has been done; much remains to be done. I believe the record not only of the past three years but of the past ten years shows that federal and provincial Governments have been organizing themselves to respond

Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to speak to the motion today regarding the need to protect adequately the Canadian environment from toxic and hazardous wastes. I am also pleased to hear the Minister say that he is willing to look at suggestions and recommendations to strengthen the role of Government, and I hope that includes strengthening the role of Parliament, in what is a very serious debate today and a very serious matter for the people of Canada.
I want to say that I live only a ten-minute walk from Lake Erie, and my riding of Erie is located in the heart of the Great Lakes Basin. So the ongoing battle to clean up the Great Lakes is of great concern to me because of the threat to the health and well-being of my constituents.
I realize to some degree the problem confronting the International Joint Commission in endeavouring to obtain the stated purpose of the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement of 1978, which is, "To retore and maintain the chemical, physical and biological integrity of the waters of the Great Lakes Basin Ecosystem, in light of the continued urban growth of this highly developed industrial and agricultural region which now has a population of over 37 million people. I not only now realize this problem, but I realized it back in December, 1979 when 1 sought and obtained the unanimous consent of this House to my motion under Standing Order 43, which read as follows:
In view of the fact that a (U.S. Company) has been dumping thousands of gallons of ... harmful chemicals into the Niagara River on a daily basis, and in view of the fact that the continuation of this method of disposal has a potentially harmful and lasting effect on the health of all citizens, Canadian and American, who live along the river. I move ... that the Government express its concern ... and urge the Government of the United States to look directly into this matter and take what action is necessary so as to alleviate the potential danger of such a continued disposal method of harmful chemicals.
Then again, on February 3, 1981 I raised this matter in the House as follows:
recent press reports . . . indicate that American industry and Government dumped toxic and radioactive wastes into the Niagara River during the Second World War. If these reports are well founded, the health of residents of the
Niagara Peninsula is seriously threatened. Therefore I move ... that this House urge the Secretary of State for External Affairs to investigate the veracity of these stories immediately and to report his findings to the House.
I am sorry to report that this motion did not receive unanimous consent.
Two countries, Mr. Speaker, with different priorities and policies have this common problem and must learn to cooperate in order to come to an agreement on measures of protection and prevention satisfactory to the people of both nations. It would apear that the original state of the Great Lakes can never be restored, but reasonable objectives are attainable. The Boundary Waters Treaty states that:
These waters whose shoreline or banks are shared by the two countries shall not be polluted on either side to the injury of health or property of the other.
Residents should expect to have pure drinking water and uncontaminated waters as well for fishing, swimming and boating. Certainly the denial of these basic rights to residents on the shores of the Great Lakes would be considered as injury of health or property.
It is disturbing to report that the levels of toxins in fish and waterfowl in this area is significantly higher than it was in 1978 when the Boundary Waters Treaty was signed. On April 15, 1981 I again raised with the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) the matter of dumping effluent into the Niagara River, and I quote:
Recent press reports indicate that as a result of malfunctions in the Buffalo sewage plant, millions of gallons of improperly treated waste are being dumped daily into the Niagara River. Therefore I move .. . that this House urge the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) to verify these reports, and upon determining their truth, to inform the United States Government immediately of Canada's deep concern about pollution in this international waterway.
I did not receive unanimous consent for this motion.
As the Member for Erie, I am concerned that little action is being taken to ensure adherence to the terms of the Boundary Waters Treaty. In July, 1982 I urged the Minister of the Environment to speed up the appointment of a third Canadian representative on the International Joint Commission so that there would be a strong Canadian voice on the Commission when such crucial issues as the clean up of the Great Lakes were being discussed. A third member has since been appointed. On January 24, 1983 the Minister of the Environment issued a press release announcing new Canadian action to investigate S-area contamination. This followed hard on the heels of an extensive Canadian federal investigation which showed that S-area poses a greater threat to Canadian waters than any other United States landfill uncovered to date.
Therefore, it seems ironic to me, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister would make this statement six weeks after the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) raised the question in the House with the Minister.
My colleague referred to the very discouraging report issued by the New York Department of Health that toxic chemicals contamination in the Lake Ontario-Niagara River Basin is increasing rather then decreasing. With more pollutants escaping now than anticipated and with the report that Canadian water treatment plants are not equipped to remove
January 27, 1983

them from drinking water, this is serious indeed. The Department of National Health and Welfare makes that alarming statement regarding the inadequacy of the Canadian water treatment plants, and considering that some of these toxic chemicals are deadly, 1 echo my colleague's question to the Minister: Has the time not yet come for an emergency Summit meeting and the establishment of an international task force?
Since 1978 the Niagara Falls, New York system has been discharging contaminated water and raw sewage containing chemicals into the lower Niagara River. The Minister is well aware of this. Also, there has been a contamination of the bedrock structure along the river. Since the Minister has been saying that the federal Government is taking some action, I want to ask him if he will table the representations which have been made in writing by either himself or the Department of External Affairs?
What is the purpose and the effect of the 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Treatment Agreement if nothing more can be done? The actions proposed in the Minister's statement are as follows: first, a study of the plume of toxic chemicals believed to be moving southward from S-Area through underground layers beneath the Niagara River and into Canadian territory; second, increased funding through the Great Lakes Water Quality Program for comprehensive analyses of drinking water quality in Lake Ontario; third, additional funds to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to conduct a comprehensive analysis of Lake Ontario fish for chemicals emanating from S-area, including dioxin; and fourth, that monitoring for chemicals in the river will be intensified to include classes of contaminants indicated as present in S-area.
I agree with the Minister and the Government that these actions are important and fine but in themselves they are not enough. I repeat, as well as these actions there should be an emergency Summit meeting and the establishment of an international task force to get Parliament involved with our United States' counterparts.
In the Minister's statement, he admits that the United States Government made public a revised complaint against Occidental Chemical Corporation, formerly the well-known Hooker Chemicals and Plastics Corporation, in late December, recognizing the seriousness of the contamination as well as the direct infiltration of S-area contaminants into the Niagara Falls, New York drinking water treatment plant.
At the conclusion of his press release, the Minister pledged that the federal Government will continue to press the U.S. for a complete clean-up of S-area and will be consulting with American officials on the development of comprehensive studies to define the extent of contaminant movement, remedial measures and the monitoring and evaluation of remedial programs.
The August, 1982 report of the International Joint Commission notes 24 different regions in the Province of Ontario that have been identified as problem areas. The Niagara and St. Clair Rivers are two of our freshwater sources which are most seriously in need of an extensive clean-up. Human health
Supply
concerns have to be given the highest priority and much more work needs to be done in eliminating the sources of pollution in these areas and undoing the damage which has already been done. Identification of problem areas alone is not enough. I repeat, it is not good enough!
On January 25, 1983 my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. Catharines, addressed the Minister's statement on the safety of drinking water, and I quote from pages 22193-4 of Hansard'.
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of the Environment who will recall answering a question of mine some six weeks ago by stating that the S-Area does not constitute a threat to the quality of the drinking water of some four million Canadians. On what basis would the Minister make such a statement to this House, and then yesterday issue a press release indicating that this S-Area is somewhat of a new and pressing problem which should be eradicated almost immediately? ... since he has had knowledge of it for some considerable length of time.
The Minister replied, in part, as follows:
There is no evidence whatsoever that the standards of drinking water in the Niagara River or Lake Ontario are beyond those which are established as being safe. There is no indication in the present situation of any conflict with the existing safe water guidelines. That does not mean we should not be concerned about leakages or the migration of fill. There are problems which should concern us.
And well they should, Mr. Speaker. In a subsequent answer the Minister said:
What is new in this situation is not changes in the quality of water; what is new is the evidence of migration, underground, of potentially dangerous products to Canadian territory. That is the new element of the situation which 1 discussed yesterday. 1 brought forward an action program which will help us deal with that.
My colleague's recommendation, and I repeat his words once again, is as follows: "The establishment of an international task force and the holding of an emergency Summit meeting with the latest findings." This must take place; this must happen.
The Globe and Mail for January 25, 1983, on page 1, reported on the leaking which turns water into "toxic brew , quoting federal scientist Douglas Hallet who said that some of the hundreds of chemicals found in the S-area dump include reactives, which can combine in the ground to form new and unknown chemicals as they mix. Mr. Hallet called the chemical brew "just as dangerous as radiation", and said it contains substances known to cause cancer, mutations and birth defects.
Mr. Hallet said he believes the dump contains dioxin, the deadliest of all chemical wastes. That is frightening. The report in The Globe and Mail goes on to say that the S-area is one of four major chemical dumps polluting the lower Niagara River. The other three, Love Canal, the Hyde Park dump and the 102nd Street dump, and dozens of other dumps, are believed to post some hazard to the region.
I want to conclude my remarks by urging the Minister to take seriously the recommendations made earlier this week by my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. Catharines. I will repeat them although I have done so earlier in my address. The Government should seriously consider the establishment of an international task force to study this immediate and most

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for recognizing me. I congratulate the NDP for bringing this very timely topic up for discussion in the House. I also note that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) is here and has been here throughout this debate. I am glad he is here to hear the comments which I will be making because they affect very specifically the Niagara Peninsula, where I live. My words will follow the comments of the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz). We have adjacent ridings and the problems we are facing now are ongoing problems which we have had for a number of years.
I would also point out, with respect, that a provincial Member of Parliament, Vince Kerrio from Niagara Falls, spearheaded the formation of a discussion and action group in
the Niagara Peninsula some six or seven years ago. The Minister nods his head because it was Mr. Kerrio and his very able research assistants who brought this particular problem of the Niagara Basin and the Niagara River to the attention, first of all, of the provincial Parliament and, of course, we have had discussions in the House on numerous occasions.
The Hon. Member for Erie states quite correctly that he and other Members from the Niagara Peninsula have brought this problem to the floor of the House by making statements, raising 43s and asking questions of the Minister, and much has been done; but there is much more that can and must be done if we are to rectify this particular problem.
In my remarks, I would like to deal, first of all, with toxic wastes generally and their disposal. Then I would like to address myself specifically to the problems we are facing in the Niagara Peninsula. Following that, I would be happy to receive questions or comments from my other colleagues and address myself to them. It was noted earlier that there were problems across Canada, but Ontario and Quebec, the most industrialized provinces, in my opinion, have done studies and uncovered worrisome problems in our own area.
We talk about the complacency of the public. I do not think there is any complacency among thinking people, but one antidote to complacency, if there is any, might be a brief consideration of polychlorinated biphenyls, the PCBs that we talk about. In concentrations of a mere one part per billion, they can kill certain living organisms. During the 50 years that they have been in use, there has been constant leakage of them into the environment as well as deliberate dumping.
Environment Canada has determined that there are over 17 million pounds of PCBs needing disposal in the Province of Ontario alone. Fortunately, almost all of these are securely stored, but in my opinion they ought to be destroyed.
Facts such as these are intimidating and even discouraging, yet they must be faced. At this moment there are over 50,000 chemicals on the market and almost 35,000 have been classified by the United States Environmental Protection Agency as being either definitely or potentially hazardous to human health. New concoctions are being developed at the rate of over 1,000 a year. These are some of the hard facts; it is not scaremongering to speak of them. If our society wants the benefits that chemicals can give us, then we must control and manage them and dispose of hazardous wastes in a responsible manner.
We must be sure that dangerous chemicals remain our servants, because once they get out of hand they become very cruel masters indeed. Toxic wastes, as mentioned by the Hon. Member for Erie and the Minister earlier, must be safely neutralized. Every barrel of waste casually sealed and stuck haphazardly into the ground becomes a ticking time bomb primed to go off at any time.
Fortunately, the news in this area is not all bad. It is gratifying to see the consensus that has developed among the public, Government and industry that the problem of hazardous
January 27, 1983

wastes must be attacked on a broad front, and soon. I am pleased that there are encouraging things to report as well.
Perhaps the easiest way to handle hazardous wastes is to ensure that they are not allowed to cause trouble in the first place. We would be well on the way toward conquering the hazardous waste problem if a proper program of monitoring toxics could be devised and instituted, with strict, so-called cradle-to-grave tracking of chemicals whose dangerous properties would be known and registered before a product came on the market, and with control systems set up to ensure that wastes are delivered only to authorized facilities. I am going to deal with that a little later in my discussion.
It is to this end that Canada strongly supports the chemical management program of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, the OECD, and we are a member of that body.
It is important to co-ordinate our tactics on the national level as well, and this is exactly what the Department of the Environment is trying to do. The proposed regulation under the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act will require the development of necessary systems and administrative arrangements between the federal and provincial transportation and environmental agencies for controlling the movement of international and interprovincial shipments of hazardous waste. We have all seen what can happen when these hazardous wastes are transferred from city to city, from Province to Province or nation to nation, and we have such a mishap as we had in Mississauga just a few years ago with the derailment of one of the trains.
Another initiative that Environment Canada has taken is the establishment of our Toxic Chemicals Management Centre. Scientists here will oversee the identification and assessment of problems caused by toxics and recommend solutions. The primary purpose of the Centre is to draw up priorities and thereby influence the allocation of those resources. I am talking about people, equipment and money which we use to deal with toxics. For example, priority lists of key chemicals or waste streams will be regularly published and updated. The idea is to anticipate needs and not just to react to those terrible emergencies which will be facing us. With the help of this Centre, the Department of the Environment, Canada's Health and Welfare Department and certain other federal Departments will co-operate in monitoring, testing, research and control activities in air, water and other programs.
Nonetheless, we still have a long way to go on the score of public confidence. While it is true that the public has often been burned, so to speak, and that chemophobia is rampant- the fear of chemicals-it is probably impossible that unanimous consent to build a treatment facility, no matter how safe, could ever be obtained anywhere.
Now 1 direct myself to what do we do with the wastes we now have on our hands? Much could be done to tell the public of the great advances in the development of safe waste technology which have already been made. We have a lot to learn from the Europeans in this regard. The waste treatment centre in Nyborg, Denmark, for example, processes waste, recovers oil and solvents, safely incinerates combustible materials and
Supply
detoxifies inorganic wastes to the maximum extent possible. Its performance satisfies the most rigorous environmental and health standards, and the treatment centre is a welcome part of its community.
Within a one kilometre radius of that plant are a public beach, a park, a golf course and a residential neighbourhood. The plant is jointly owned by Government and industry and is integrated into a total system which includes the sites that produce the waste and a collection network. Such treatment centres could provide local employment and serve as magnets to attract industry, all in an environmentally safe manner. It is not at all utopian to speak of such facilities. They already exist and are already in service.
Some three weeks ago I had representatives of just such a company come to see me. Its head offices are located in the Niagara Peninsula, but it operates throughout Ontario and Canada. Its representatives explained what can be done with these hazardous wastes and how to dispose of them safely. I have set up a further interview with them and I am going to tour the plant in the very near future. I am happy this company is located in my area and I am happy it is giving us some of the answers that we so desperately need concerning the problem of waste management.
We have greatly increased our ability to recycle waste, and the capability to detoxify safely or incinerate hazardous waste is, for all practical purposes, right here and now, at hand. This is' a matter of will. Society must shoulder the burden of responsibility for the life style it demands, a life style made possible by chemicals.
One expert in the field has remarked that we have technical solutions for waste problems, but what we do not have are the social solutions. Everyone is in favour of a safe landfill site, but not in his or her home town. There is even a term for this attitude; perhaps Hon. Members have heard of it. It is called the NIMBY syndrome, which is short for "Not in my back yard". The NIMBY attitude will and must be overcome.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, this attitude is all too understandable, especially given events of the type that have been going on in our own back yards, especially in the ridings of the Hon. Members for Erie, Niagara Falls (Mr. MacBain), Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), as well as my own, that of Welland, which are here in Ontario and in the Niagara Basin. I am referring to cross-boundary pollution, since this is an area that is obviously a federal responsibility.
The chemical waste situation in the Niagara area, as was pointed out by the provincial member for Niagara Falls, Vince Kerrio, could well serve as a microcosm for the entire problem. One can recite the whole dreary litany that we have all come to know so well: disposal of toxic wastes in a manner that conformed to standard practice decades ago but has now proved to be grossly inadequate; lack of co-ordination between Government and industry planners; a public that feels it has been kept in the dark and is now embittered and rightly so;

January 27, 1983
Supply
constant and paralyzing wrangling over who is or is not at fault and who is to pay for the clean-up. I think the people of our area and across Canada have had their fill of that; the script has been all too predictable.
The situation is further complicated by the fact that three levels of Government are involved on each side of the border. When we have to bring this many groups together, we can see that the problems multiply accordingly.
The real tragedy in all this, of course, is that while lawyers argue over responsibility, and while debates about who is to pay drag on and on, the hazardous chemicals that have leached into the water table are constantly continuing their insidious work.

In Welland, in my riding, which is not as close to the Niagara River where all this is going on, a number of people from the riding are working on this problem. In fact, in Welland, our drinking water comes from the same river, and in all sincerity, Mr. Speaker, plans are not enough. We must have action, based on what we know today, and we must do whatever is necessary to destroy the toxic wastes the river contains, which are causing illness in our area.

Take two examples. First, the Hyde Park landfill in Niagara Falls, New York. From 1953 to 1975, 80,000 tonnes of chemical wastes, including materials contaminated with dioxin, were deposited at this location. Dioxin has been detected in the sediments of the creek leading from the site to the Niagara River itself.
Second, the Niagara Falls sewage treatment plant in New York which was mentioned by the Minister. This is a plant that began operation in December, 1977. Almost from the start it had serious problems, and its carbon absorption beds were taken out of operation after only six months. Because of this, effluent, both human and industrial, is discharged into the Niagara River after what I and many people believe to be inadequate treatment.
Regrettably, and I must say this to the Minister and to all colleagues in the House, the steps being taken to rectify the situation at the plant are proceeding much too slowly. Even if a decision were made tomorrow about what steps are to be taken to correct the situation, we still would not be out of the woods because an adequate plant would not be fully operational for at least two years after the first day remedial work began. Meanwhile, waste of every description is pouring into our waters. In its efforts to stay on top of the situation, Canada has asked repeatedly for assurance that the various water quality agreements will not be violated, and it has also asked for co-operation in monitoring the river so that we will be able to tell exactly what hazardous wastes are contaminating our waters.
The Department of the Environment staff actually did their own sampling for the Niagara Falls sewage treatment plant. Environment Canada has had to invest an extraordinary amount of time and resources to maintain a watching brief on
the progress of these issues. Studies carried out in May, 1981 give us great cause for concern. They confirm that pollutants are not being adequately treated before discharge into the Niagara River. In all, 41 organic compounds and heavy metals were indicated in the samples taken. These include 25 priority pollutants named by the Environmental Protection Agency in the United States.
Mr. Speaker and my colleagues, I do not mean to imply that we Canadians are guilt-free when it comes to polluting the Great Lakes with hazardous wastes. There are far too many sources of pollution on our side of the border as well. We must take the responsibility for what we have done to our Great Lakes and to our rivers. Nonetheless, it is a cold fact that, when all dischargers within the Niagara River's watershed are considered, the total United States point source discharge exceeds total Canadian discharge by more than two billion litres a day. Let me repeat that. The total U.S. point source discharge exceeds total Canadian discharge by more than two billion litres a day.
This is not acceptable. This cannot go on in this, one of the most highly populated areas of Canada. It cannot be allowed to go unchecked, and this applies to both sides of the border. I call upon the Minister, his cabinet colleagues as well as all my colleagues in the House to refrain from making this a partisan issue. This is a Canadian issue, one which all of us must address.
While we must be realistic in facing these facts, there is no need to give only the gloom and doom despair side of it. Environment Canada has established a firm foundation on which to base our efforts for effective waste management in the Niagara region. There are many precedents for fruitful international co-operation in the Great Lakes Basin. The recent consultations with the U.S. Government on the subject of dioxin provide but one example.
We have an effective monitoring and tracking program already in place and can analyze and track pollutants to their source with a great deal of precision. Laws are already on the books that can force polluters to clean up their act and manage hazardous waste in a responsible manner. Perhaps most important of all, the federal Government has demonstrated that it is willing, even anxious, to join with provincial and local Governments, and with the United States, in a co-ordinated effort to solve the crisis in waste management that so urgently confronts us.
I ask that all Members put aside bi-partisari ideas with regard to this pollution problem. I ask that we join together in asking, urging and demanding that our Minister and this Government act positively to solve this problem as soon as possible.

Madam Speaker, this House settles most matters or issues by division. Such is the nature or foundation of the parliamentary system of Government. However, one of the most fundamental processes also used for action is unanimous consent of all Members of the House on matters falling within our constitutional bounds. This action by unanimous consent is perhaps the most fundamental basis of our democratic system of Government.
Equally vital, and perhaps the second most fundamental right and privilege of the House and its Members, is the ability to put before the House a matter of urgent and/or pressing

speechtext:

Since that time he has become a world-wide symbol of resistance to Soviet efforts to stamp out fundamental human rights.

exemption urged for charitable organizations

Madam Speaker, the federal Government has refused the rescind its excise tax on publications distributed by the Canadian Cancer Society and other charities. As a result, between $50,000 and $100,000 a year in donations to the Canadian Cancer Society will go to the Government rather than to research and education, which is what the Society is all about in the first place.
I am concerned about the statement that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) made whereby he made it appear as though the excise tax was confined to imported materials. In actual fact the Society informed the Minister on March 12, 1982, that an estimated 90 per cent of the problems of the Canadian Cancer Society relate to federal sales tax on Canadian produced materials rather than imports. Clearly, the Minister is misinformed and, as a result of that misinformation, the volunteers who are the backbone of the Society continue to have an added burden which could be lightened if the federal Government would move in this matter.
I ask the Government to respond to this request. Specifically, I ask it to pass an immediate remission order which would exempt Canadian charities, including the Canadian Cancer Society, from federal sales tax on Canadian produced materials, or to effect such a change in the budget to be brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) this spring.

Madam Speaker, Members of the House and the Government know that the North American market essentially establishes prices for farm commodity products and, more precisely, that Canadian products such as corn and soy beans find their prices set on the Chicago market. Input costs in Canada are essentially exactly the same as those of the American producers, and find themselves, in large instance, established by the prices of inputs such as sprays and fertilizers which have natural gas or petroleum as their base.
A few years ago the border was closed to Canadian farmers importing those products, in order to try to help create a Canadian industry. Without reflecting on whether or not that cause has been established, and whether that end has been met, we now find that U.S. prices for those input costs, particularly fertilizers and herbicide sprays, have been going down dramatically over the last year, whereas in Canada the same companies are producing the same products for Canadian farmers at the maintained high prices without seeing any fall. It is time that a message go from this House and this Government to those companies to indicate that Canadian producers must have equality, and that prices must fall or the border will be reopened.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to address the House on an important matter to which reference has already been made by the Hon. Member for Don Valley East (Mr. Smith), that is, in connection with Anatoly Shcharansky.
Mr. Shcharansky has been in prison for six years, a large part of it in solitary confinement and, worse, in the confinement of a punishment cell. He has endured the ravages of a hunger strike, the pain of forced feeding, and the deprivation of any human contact with his family, particularly with his aged and ill mother who, herself, has undergone many hardships in her vain attempts to see her son.
I would urge the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to appeal on behalf of the Government, Parliament and the people of Canada, directly to the Leader of the Soviet Union, Mr. Andropov, that Mr. Shcharansky's case be reconsidered on humanitarian grounds and that the Soviet Union see fit to allow Shcharansky his freedom and permission to join his wife outside the Soviet Union.
