subtopic: EFFECT OF PROPOSAL TO ELIMINATE SPOUSAL DEDUCTION
EFFECT OF PROPOSAL TO ELIMINATE SPOUSAL DEDUCTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians continue to protest recent irresponsible statements by the Minister responsible for the status of women. Her call for the elimination of tax exemptions for spouses would cause financial hardships for families, older couples, and single parents. Poor women would be deprived of benefits because they pay no income tax. It is not too late for the Minister to apologize publicly for her insulting putdown of women who contribute to society through their unpaid work in the home and the community.
The New Democratic Party believes there must be tax reforms to benefit low and middle-income families. Highest income earners must pay their fair share. This would provide funds for tax credits and increased family allowances. We ask that a major review of federal income programs and tax benefits for families be undertaken to determine the most equitable means of paying compensation to the principal parenting person. Benefits should be adjusted to family needs, whether or not the parent works in or out of the home. Women must have choices with access to jobs and to affordable child care.

subtopic: UNFAVOURABLE WEATHER CONDITIONS-CONSEQUENCES FOR QUEBEC APPLE GROWERS
UNFAVOURABLE WEATHER CONDITIONS-CONSEQUENCES FOR QUEBEC APPLE GROWERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Quebec apple growers have suffered tremendous losses in their orchards as a result of unfavourable weather conditions during the winter of 1980-1981. A study made in August, 1982 by Agriculture Canada showed that 31 per cent of our standard apple trees died, which means 291,000 trees. Although all apple producing areas in Quebec were affected, the number of apple growers who were severely affected was highest in the orchards north of Montreal and around Missisquoi.
On December 15, 1982, representatives of the Federation des producteurs de pommes du Quebec had a meeting in Ottawa with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture and representatives of the various agricultural
Oral Questions
organizations concerned, and submitted a complete file on the losses suffered by the Canadian apple-growing industry as a result of unfavourable weather conditions during the winter of 1980-81.
Madam Speaker, our apple growers hope the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will soon make a decision in their favour, providing urgently needed financial assistance and thus preventing a number of bankruptcies.

subtopic: IMPACT OF TAXES ON ALBERTA CO-OPERATIVE
IMPACT OF TAXES ON ALBERTA CO-OPERATIVE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Bow River Gas Co-op in Alberta, with some 600 members, covers approximately 2,300 square miles, has 180,000 acres under irrigation, and 60,000 acres of dryland farming. The burden placed on these farmers by the National Energy Program and federal taxes is an excellent illustration of why the farmers of Canada are so depressed, and of why more than 400 farmers went bankrupt last year.
Farming and the high cost of energy go hand in hand. This Co-op irrigates 180,000 acres by mechanical means with the use of natural gas; 27,000 tons of fertilizer produced by natural gas were used on 240,000 acres, and the tax on the natural gas used was $1,134,000,000. In addition, the Co-op paid the federal Government $270,000. The Canadian Western Natural Gas Company, which supplied part of the area with natural gas, paid the federal Government $513,000 in direct taxes. All of these federal taxes have to be added to the cost of production, plus the provincial and municipal taxes, with the result that there will be more and more farm bankruptcies and less production as farmers will not be able to fertilize their land. If the Liberal Government is sincere in wanting to keep food plentiful and our farms in operation, it better be realistic and remove this excessive tax on natural gas.

subsubtopic: PAY TV-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON TELEVISING OF PORNOGRAPHY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Communications. For the last three weeks the Minister and the Chairman of the CRTC have played ping-pong with the very serious issue of sexual violence, stereotyping and degradation of women over Pay TV. All of us realize that broadcasting is a federal matter, but we have reached the ludicrous position where the federal Government and federal regulators and policy makers refuse to take responsibility for what is going on.
The CRTC Chairman's non-solution is that he will get together a group of the producers of porn and they will regulate themselves. To make matters worse, the Commission's draft regulations on Pay TV do not contain the protection which now exists for AM and FM Radio or broadcasting, dealing with indecent or profane material, and the protection of minority groups.
My question is simply this. Is it the Government's policy, through its inaction, to give tacit approval to a pornographic television industry in Canada? If not, then what does the Minister intend to do about it?

subsubtopic: PAY TV-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON TELEVISING OF PORNOGRAPHY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I really wonder where the Hon. Member has been for the last week and a half. On a number of occasions Members on this side of the House, and a Member of his own caucus, have raised the question time and time again. We, as a Government, indicated very real concern, and we also indicated a number of steps which could possibly be taken. Therefore I am really quite delighted that yesterday afternoon the CRTC issued a public statement calling for all Pay TV licensees to come in and meet with them to examine this whole question and establish guidelines.
Furthermore, the statement indicates quite clearly that they are reviewing proposed Pay Television network regulations, taking into account concerns expressed relating to sexual exploitation. They go on to say that they subscribe to the philosophy expressed in the recommendation made by the task force on sex role stereotyping to the CRTC, notably Section 3, which includes the statement that the Commission should also discourage the portrayal of gratuitous violence against women and expect Pay Television licensees to do the same.
If the Hon. Member reads the public notice issued yesterday by the Chairman of the CRTC, or the press release issued at that time, I think it is quite clear that the CRTC is very much concerned about some of the developments aired in this House by Members on both sides, and is indeed taking the action it ought to take under the Broadcasting Act.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Fulton:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to adequately protect the Canadian environment from toxic and hazardous waste and for its subservience to the vested interests of the chemical and industrial waste producers and, in particular, for its failure to expedite the clean-up of the Great Lakes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, prior to the lunch break I asked Members on both sides of the House, including the Minister, if there would be agreement to permit me to table a report that was put together by a group of Members from my caucus. This document is entitled "An Environmental Task Force: A Report on Toxic Chemical Pollution".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: It is not a very good report.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
I want to thank Hon. Members for allowing me to table this document. I just wanted to say that before I start
January 27, 1983

my remarks this afternoon. I would suggest, though, that the Liberal Member on the other side who probably has not yet had an opportunity to read the report do so, because he would probably be a much more informed Member if he does that.
We had a repeat performance by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) at the end of Question Period of the kind of performance to which we have become accustomed on this issue in the last two or three-year period. Questions were put to the Minister primarily by Members on this side of the House, particularly myself and the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), who is the mover of the Motion before the House today. The Minister's response has perhaps been expected in the past, but I would have thought from his statements earlier this week, wherein he seemed to indicate that his mind had been opened and he had suddenly become aware there was a problem in the Niagara Peninsula, that he would not have proceeded with the same kind of political put-downs, or attempted put-downs, that he had utilized in the past in an effort to dismiss the seriousness of this matter. It is not enough to address that particular problem with statements such as "If you ask questions on this you are nothing but an alarmist. You people in the NDP are scaring people. It is totally irresponsible to raise this question in the House."
The Minister has gone to the point where he advised us in response to a question from me that we were talking through our hats and did not know what we were talking about. We have become used to those kinds of statements from the Minister, disappointing though as they may be. I suppose we are expected to absorb that in the natural course of things. I expect the Minister to do that, although I am disappointed that he does so.
I object, as one Liberal mentioned earlier in the debate today, when people who are attempting to express their concerns in their communities and find answers about possible hazards to the health of people who live in those communities or, in this case, whether Lake Ontario is a safe source of drinking water, are put down by politicians and bureaucrats and dismissed as being NIMBYs. I am sure that is a new word to most Members in the House but it is one that is used quite extensively to dismiss people in those communities as being either reactionary or at least irresponsible in terms of their perceived obligation toward a Government initiative and their support of that initiative. A NIMBY, as some bureaucrats like to label a number of citizens, stands for the "Not in my back yard" syndrome. That is the kind of put-down that is made to dismiss the concerns which many of those persons have about the possible dangers of chemical dump sites or other Government programs to their immediate family and community.
In the course of the Minister's remarks earlier today, he attempted again to dispel the very real dangers that exist as a result of the chemical wastes which are leaching from the dump sites on the New York State side into the Niagara Gorge, the Niagara River and on into Lake Ontario. He continues today, as he has over the past several years, to say
Supply
that there is no evidence that this is happening. I suggest to the Minister that, quite to the contrary, there is sufficient evidence which clearly shows that dioxin, the most dangerous chemical known to man, is leaching from those chemical dump sites into the Niagara River and on into the drinkig water supply of the residents around Lake Ontario. Even Members of his own Department, some of whom are very qualified individuals, have confirmed this fact.
I might note for Hon. Members that dioxin is so dangerous that an individual from the Minister's Department has estimated that a shovel full of that chemical dumped into Lake Ontario would kill the entire lake. Yet it is being allowed to leach into the lake uncontrolled as a result of the Minister's inaction in demanding a political intervention with politicians on the American side of the border.
During the course of our investigation into this matter, officials from the Environmental Protection Agency in the United States told us quite bluntly that the Reagan administration was not becoming overly concerned about this question and was prepared to sit back and listen unduly to the chemical industry in the United States because Canada is not applying enough political pressure on the U.S. Government to make it confront the problem. The Government has merely passed diplomatic notes to the United States up to this point as a political response to this problem. This does not include some of the testing which has been carried out in the Niagara Peninsula recently. The Government's only political response so far has been to lightly slap the U.S. administration on the wrist and ask it to take action. Frankly, the United States Government will not take action until the Canadian Government demands that it do so.
We asked some members of the New York State Assembly to outline for us what they thought the problems were. The Environmental Committee of the New York State Assembly met with us when we were in Niagara Falls. To our great surprise, they did not engage in any rhetoric as the Minister is prone to do. They were not interested in blaming Canada or the U.S. Government for the problem. Instead, they considered it an issue which must be approached in a non-partisan manner. They agreed that the pollution should be cleaned up and were not interested in making political points on the issue. In fact, they told us that their committee had invited our Minister of the Environment to appear before them so they could hear the Canadian concerns directly and raise them with their colleagues. We were told that the Minister of the Environment refused to speak to them. He said that this issue was not on his list of priorities. He was more concerned, to use their term, with the sexy issue of acid rain. One must wonder, particularly after listening to the answers to questions we have asked the Minister in the House, whether there is a perception on that side of the House that there are more political or Brownie points to be made on acid rain than on the question of toxic waste pollution of our lake system.

speechtext:
He is not doing anything about acid rain.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: As my colleague for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) reminds me, the Minister is not doing much about acid rain either, even after the establishment of a task force of Members of the House. They made an extensive investigation into the problems of acid rain and tabled an excellent and well-documented report in the House which spells out the problem very well. However, the Minister is still incapable of taking action. I am beginning to wonder if that Minister is a political eunuch in terms of his responsibility in his portfolio.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: And he wants to be leader.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
And he wants to be the leader of his Party. Good luck to them.
I should remind the House that we conducted our investigation with very limited research support. We used our own staff members who admittedly only had layman's experience on the question. However, we discovered facts that the Minister did not seem to have. When we presented these facts to his environmental officials, they accepted those facts and indicated that on their superficial examination of them they believed that we gathered information in one week that was as accurate as theirs. I am not discrediting those officials for I believe they have done a tremendous job under the circumstances.
For example, we found that in Lake Ontario alone there are 400 known, identified chemicals that simply come from industrial waste pollution. One chemical on its own, in isolation, may or may not cause a problem, but the burning question out there involves the fact that no one knows because no one has studied it. No one knows what effect the combination of any of those 400 chemicals will have on one another. We all know that one chemical on its own may be a stable element, but we do not know what happens when different chemicals combine.
No one has ever done any study on that subject, and I think it should be done for a number of reasons. First, it is the Minister's responsibility to ensure that that drinking water is safe for the people who consume it; second, it is necessary in order to satisfy the concerns which have been expressed by people in Ontario and by politicians in the House on their behalf.
There is absolutely no question but that these problems are very real and they exist. I mentioned the Minister's officials earlier on and said that I did not want to criticize them because I think they do a good job under the circumstances. I want to tell Hon. Members that when Hooker Chemicals was before the U.S. court concerning the American Government's attempt to force it to clean up its act, our Government would not even intervene before the court. One of the Minister's top officials was forced to take his vacation time in order to give expert testimony in the U.S. court about what was happening to Lake Ontario. That is what a conscientious public employee whose boss would not even allow him to go in the name of the Department had to do. I think that is shameful on the part of the Minister and it is a damn disgrace on the part of the
Government, especially when one considers some of the expert testimony which was given to us.
For example, Dr. Berkes, Professor of Urban and Environmental Studies at Brock University, told us this in St. Catharines:
The Environmental Baseline Study of the Niagara River issued in 1980, concluded that water taken from Niagara-on-the-Lake, Niagara Falls and Fort Erie met "federal and provincial criteria for acceptable drinking water".
The report does not add that drinking water quality in these waters was within guidelines only because there are no guidelines for a vast number of potentially hazardous chemical substances.
Assurances that drinking water meet Government standards are misleading and irresponsible.
Again, in terms of the attempted put-down concerning people who are asking questions about this serious matter and are referred to as being "NIMBY" or persons afflicted with the NIMBY syndrome, Professor Farka, Professor of Man-Environmental Studies at the University of Waterloo, stated the following in a brief he presented to our task force:
In fact, the situation is quite different. The factual situation is that the major industrial liquid waste proposals made in Ontario to-date have been inadequate and incomplete on technical grounds. Thus it is no wonder that they have been rejected on a combination of technical, social, political, and environmental grounds. Those who use the NIMBY Syndrome for the failure of these proposals are in fact using NIMBY as a scapegoat to cover the inadequacies of these proposals.
During the course of one week we talked to residents who have been voicing their concern over the last several years about what is happening in the Niagara River. We attended public meetings and went to these people's homes, speaking to them individually. I want to ensure the House that those individuals to whom we spoke were expressing a common concern. Some of them were rather fearful that they would have to raise their children in that particular community because of the unanswered questions concerning the safety of the drinking water supply, and that fear was not alarmist, it was very real. I am sure that if the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. MacBain) rises to speak in the debate, he can confirm that these are extremely rational, sane people. The arguments they presented to us were, for the most part, not emotional; they were very reasoned and well thought out. They had done their own research and had listened to people from the scientific community. This experience extremely impressed myself and my colleagues on that particular committee.
I will repeat what I said during Question Period, and I meant it sincerely. The Minister responsible for this particular Department should do no less than accept his full responsibility to the Canadian people and to this House. He should insist upon a meeting between himself and the Governor of New York State, and should sit down and rationally discuss this question and come to some form of an agreement to clean this situation up for the safety of all Canadians.

speechtext:
I claim some understanding of the frustrations, having been the spokesman for our Party on matters of environment for two or three years. It is a very frustrating experience because one is so seldom able to get the matter on the floor of the House. One sees the Government moving very slowly or not at all. One is exposed to all kinds of citizen pressure, both from individuals and groups. I understand all of those frustrations and I compliment him for bringing the matter before us.
At this stage in the debate, I doubt that the issue needs any definition, but that will not deter me. I think other Hon.
Supply
Members will have shared with me the experience of the Time magazine cover story of September, 1980, about two and a half years ago. It was a very compelling story. If it helps to define that which they say may not need defining, I wish to quote from it. It is entitled "The Poisoning of America". I will quote briefly from the opening paragraph as follows:
Of all of man's interventions in the natural order, none is accelerating quite so alarmingly as the creation of chemical compounds. Through their genius, modern alchemists brew as many as 1,000 new concoctions each year in the U.S. alone. At last count, nearly 50,000 chemicals were on the market. Many have been an undeniable boon to mankind, mitigating pain and disease, prolonging life for millions and expanding the economy in myriad ways by stimulating the creation of new products. There is, however, a price to pay for an industrial society that has come to rely so heavily on chemicals: almost 35,000 of those used in the U.S. are classified by the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) as being either definitely or potentially hazardous to human health.
Therefore we, as part of the North American continent, have these very obvious and dramatic problems. First, in some cases there is our inability to even identify the chemical and its toxic nature. Second, we are unable to control the introduction of these chemicals into the environment. Third, we are unable to determine how long the toxicity lasts or how pervasive these chemicals are in terms of their toxicity. Part of the problem is this enormous uncertainty.
One thing is certain. We in North America have on our hands an extraordinarily complex problem, one which will cost enormous sums, not only to clean up now but to control in the future. The dramatic example, of course, has been in the Niagara Peninsula. Much of the debate today has centred on that. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) used much of his allotted time to deal with that issue. As I understood it, his proposition was that the present administration in the United States has caved in to business interests. He may be right. I have nothing to substantiate that. He obviously feels very strongly, and he may be correct. It may even go beyond that. It has been the unhappy and maybe the necessary experience of many of us that in times of economic stress, Government expenditure in certain areas, one of which is the environment, is often the first casualty.
Therefore, I am not prepared to admit to the argument advanced by the Hon. Member that the total fault lies with big business. Part of the problem may be simply the economic recession we are now in. Whatever the cause of the failure of the United States to fulfil what I believe to be its obligations under the Canada-U.S. Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement, we do have this problem.
In my view, the Canada-U.S. Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement has been breached. I put this to the Minister following his intervention in the debate. The agreement called, first, for a projected rate of clean-up and, second, for the commitment of funds to accomplish the clean-up at that projected rate. I do not believe that either of those conditions have been met, either the rate of clean-up or the funds to accomplish this.

January 27, 1983
Supply
The Minister said that the situation is improving. When I had an opportunity to question him, 1 put to him that I very much doubt that that is the yardstick by which we should judge our performance. In my view, the yardstick is whether that water quality agreement has been fulfilled in terms of its time performance and its funding to accomplish the time performance.
Were I as a Minister to judge the performance, I would do it on the basis of that agreement and not on the fact that on a certain date certain chemicals had less presence in the Great Lakes than last year, the year before or ten years ago. There is a very clear document by which we can judge our performance and that of our southern neighbours.
Incidentally, in other areas the situation is not improving. As I say, we focused on the Great Lakes. There are other areas. I think of acid rain. I have been the very fortunate owner of a log cabin on a Northern Ontario lake which is springfed. When I go to that cabin now, I am presented with a booklet which says how much fish out of this lake I can eat. I am not threatened. I never catch fish that big, which is an admission of my frailties as a fisherman.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext: Or the judgment of the fish.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENT
speechtext:
Or the judgment of the fish, as my hon. friend points out. To receive a booklet which states how many pickerel I can eat in a certain period of a certain size and to come to the dock and see a great, big, black, red and white sign erected by either the Department of the Environment or the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, portrays dramatically and graphically how much fish I or a visiting American tourist can eat.
That has some rather serious economic consequences. If I were an American tourist visiting Northern Ontario for the first time with my wife and young children to see nature because in my country it had been devastated, I am not sure that I would be content and peaceful having my family spend their holiday period at a lake which is posted like that.
That lake is 100 miles away from Sudbury. Whether that is the cause, I do not know. I am not saying it is the big business interests in Sudbury that are causing me concern about a lake that I have loved and cherished for almost 30 years. I do not know. However, when the Minister, all of a sudden, says that things are improving, I say to him that they are sure not improving in some places. They sure are not improving in many lakes in Northern Ontario.
I understand the focus on the Niagara Peninsula. My family were fruit farmers in Grimsby. The Niagara Peninsula is my heritage. I know it and love it. I can understand the focus that has to be on it, but may I say it goes beyond that.
With respect to our relationship with the United States Government, State governments and agencies, the Minister has had the luxury of an economic recession. The publication covers such matters as, what are hazardous wastes; where do they come from; why they are such a big problem; the environmental and health considerations; the large volume of them; the limited number of treatment and disposal facilities; the fact that there is no magical solution; the technology. It even goes on to deal with the Danish example, and the Hon. Member dealt with that at some length in his remarks. As I read this whole document, I think the bottom line is that our main problem, despite some problems in technology, is the political problem. I will just quote from page 7 of that Departmental publication which reads:
-the technology for treatment of hazardous wastes is immediately available. The difficult issue is to decide where the treatment facilities should be located and where the end products of the treatment process are to be deposited, presumably in chemical landfill sites.
The solution to the problems of location will involve some public debate and compromise.
We talk about the the NIMBY syndrome, "not in my back yard". Nobody wants a hazardous waste deposit site in his back yard. Were it to come into Perth County, 1 would be the first on my feet on a point of order, in Question Period, during proceedings under Standing Order 21, the "Late Show", and everything else. residential area. I think there is a recreational facility close by, and so on. In any event, I suppose it is not much different a community than many communities in my riding or any other Member's riding which is in a rural or semi-urban area.

speechtext:
When I was interrupted, Mr. Speaker, I was referring to the problem of phosphorus in the Great Lakes Basin and the tributaries that flow into it. Phosphorus was identified as the key nutrient element which spawned the growth of nuisance algae. These algae bloomed in the summer and then sank to the lake bottoms or washed up on our shorelines. As it rotted it used up the precious store of dissolved oxygen critical to the support of aquatic life. Also as it rotted it released some more phosphorous into the lakes which further exacerbated the problem. The problem was so severe that in the late summer large portions of the bottom waters were totally devoid of dissolved oxygen.
Studies undertaken by Canadian and American scientists had determined that the reduction of phosphorous was the key factor in stemming this uncontrolled growth cycle known as an accelerated state of eutrophication.
In signing the 1972 Canada-U.S. agreement, immediate phosphorous control was a primary objective, and Canada proceeded to take the following actions. First, Canada pressed for and gained agreement with the United States to set phosphorous target levels for Lake Erie and Lake Ontario. To achieve these lower levels, the countries then agreed on an equitable reduction of phosphorous inputs.
The Canadian strategy was twofold. We would remove phosphorous from municipal sewage treatment plants and limit phosphorous contents in household laundry detergents. In 1970 and 1973 phosphorous content in laundry detergents was limited to 5 per cent and 2.2 per cent respectively under the federal Canada Water Act. Canada and Ontario undertook a successful $6 million research and development effort from 1972 to 1976 to build phosphorous removal facilities in sewage treatment plants. As a result of this effort and the accelerated funding for the construction of sewage treatment plants, all plants with a capacity greater than one million gallons per day discharging directly into the lakes were provided with phosphorous removal facilities. This was accomplished co-operatively with the Province of Ontario.
We must remember that phosphorous control on the Canadian side was only achieved because of a massive effort in building and updating sewage treatment plants at the estimated cost of SI.3 billion by all levels of Government in Canada.
January 27, 1983

By comparison, the United States has spent some $7 billion, which we would expect, given their greater population of the Great Lakes Basin. This huge investment of resources under the 1972 agreement has paid off in concrete results. These are, one, in 1972 an estimated 80 per cent of the sewer population in the Canadian portion of the Great Lakes Basin was served by sewage treatment facilities adequate to meet the water quality objectives of the agreement, including phosphorous removal. Today this figure has increased to 99 per cent.
Statistically, significant decreases in total phosphorous levels in localized areas of Lake Ontario have been achieved since 1972. Springtime concentrations along most of the north shore have dropped an average of 12 per cent. In a 20 mile stretch in the Toronto area, the decline is estimated to be 35 per cent. The decrease in chlorophyll, a measure of algae growth, in Lake Ontario has resulted in cleaner water and better swimming conditions.
In 1977, Canada essentially met the target set for phosphorous discharges from municipal waste treatment plants on Lake Erie.
Decline in phosphorous concentrations has been noted in the nearshore of the western basin of Lake Erie and at the mouth of the Detroit River. Chloride and iron concentrations, plus suspended and dissolved solids loads, are also decreasing in the river.
The average total phosphorous concentrations along the south Indiana shoreline of Lake Michigan have declined to levels comparable to those of the open lake.
Studies have provided a basis for determining the magnitude and sources of contamination to the lakes from land use activities. Recommendations of the International Joint Commission as to the remedial programs appropriate to addressing these problems are pending now.
Under the 1978 Canada and United States agreement, the parties capitalized on increased knowledge of phosphorous pollution. Further measures were instituted in the new agreement to control phosphorous from non-point sources and atmospheric deposition of phosphorous. At present this Government is finalizing a supplemental annex to the 1978 agreement with the United States which calls for controls of phosphorous from urban and agricultural runoff. These new requirements, which will be presented to Cabinet shortly, will call for a further reduction of 2,000 tons in the Lake Erie Basin and approximately 1,200 tons in the Lake Ontario Basin. The achievement of these reductions will be pursued in the most cost effective manner. Happily, the upper lakes are not threatened by eutrophication at this time due to low concentrations of population living around them. We are, however, mindful of the necessity to maintain their quality; therefore target loads have been developed for Lake Huron and Lake Superior and are currently being finalized by both parties.
The efforts that this Government has successfully put forward in combatting eutrophication is no small accomplishment. Lake Erie is alive and mending. The prognosis for Lake
Supply
Ontario is also good as far as eutrophication is concerned. While our attention has been rightly diverted to the problem of toxic chemical contamination, it is good to know that we have met the challenge with regard to phosphorous control.
I said at the beginning that my riding was particularly concerned about pollution in the Niagara River and the Great Lakes Basin. I see the Hon. Minister of the Environment is back in the House, and perhaps I can remind him directly that I do hope he will continue his financial support of Operation Clean, which is a voluntary organization in Niagara-on-the-Lake, which is also in my riding. Hopefully, notwithstanding the present restraint program in Ottawa, additional financial support will be found for Operation Clean, because they are the ones at the moment who are in the fight at the S-dump hearings. Any support, financial and otherwise, that can be given to Operation Clean by the Government of Canada will be appreciated by myself and by all Members of this House who are genuinely interested in controlling pollution in the Niagara River and the Great Lakes Basin.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRON MENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to enter this debate and to follow my friend, the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls (Mr. MacBain). I listened with great interest to what he had to say concerning the dreadful problem that we in this part of Ontario only read about rather than live in the midst of and experience. I am certain there is a great deal of worry and concern in the Niagara Falls area.
Let me preface my next remarks by saying that I am pleased the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) rose and indicated that some further funding would be available to the group dealing with the S-dump hearing called "Operation Clean." He anticipated what I was going to say. Sometimes Ministers in these times of restraint look for rupport for worthwhile undertakings from other Parties in the House of Commons. I happen to represent, at least today, another Party in the House of Commons, and had he not said that, I would have indicated my support for him. Nevertheless, I want the Minister and my hon. friend from Niagara Falls to know they have my support.
I think it is very important that we should not lose sight, even in a period of restraint, of the importance of the priority with respect to the environment and what it can do for us in terms of the quality of life in our country.
I am certain that groups in Niagara Falls who have been working on the matter must be very pleased. I am sure the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls is also very pleased.
I hope I am not being unkind to our friends in the United States by saying that I suppose what has happened to the pollution control plant that will not be put back in place in Niagara Falls, New York, until 1984, is something being repeated again and again in various parts of the United States because of the policy of the United States Government with respect to its priorities. I do not think we should necessarily criticize a Government of another country for a particular policy, but we should never allow that Government to be unmindful of the danger that we, as their neighbours to the north, regard that kind of breakdown and change in a relationship. I think that is the case. Following the State of the Union message and the results of the State Congressional elections in the United States, I suspect that, notwithstanding the fact that there are protestations to the contrary by the President of the United States that his policy has not changed, in fact, a change is coming.
There must have been a message ot the Government and the administration of the United States as a result of those elections. If I may put it in my own terms, the message was that there is something else just as important, or at least to be considered, as the balance sheet in the setting of priorities. I regard that as the message that has come as a result of some of the changes I have read and heard about recently in U.S. policy.
This reminds me of a good story told me by the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). There was a person in his riding who did not want to be seen walking into a public house or a place where alcoholic beverages are served. What he did was to walk backwards into the public house. If somebody took this person's picture it would look as if he were walking out. I have a feeling that what appears to be the United States policy of staying the course is not quite so, and that perhaps the importance of the environment and the importance of preserving the environment in the United States will now come to the fore. If the environment becomes important to American policy makers, we will be the beneficiary of some of those changes.
I regret very much what the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls said about the breach by the United States of the 1978 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. That is very serious for Canada. I believe its importance should be brought home
January 27, 1983

day by day in this forum and in other forums, using all the facilities we have.
I have differences of opinion with the Minister of the Environment from time to time, but I support him and 1 say to the House that I believe he is personally and absolutely committed to the cause of improving the environment, whether in Niagara Falls or elsewhere.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRON MENT
speechtext:
1 have served in a government and I know that from time to time one's own personal commitments are sometimes sublimated within the problems that governments face. I suspect that if it is seen in the House, and perhaps as it has been alleged in the House, that there has not been a great enough push with the United States and in Canada concerning environmental problems, much of that lack has to do with the priorities set by the Government as a whole.
A cabinet Minister with a government is not independent. He is subject to the eventual setting of priorities by a government as a whole, and we must remember that. However, the Minister of the Environment is absolutely committed to this issue. Those who worry in times of great trouble that we must concentrate on the bottom line and ignore every other consideration, are wrong. There are countries much more troubled economically than Canada that have taken another view.
In the United Kingdom, notwithstanding its great financial difficulties, there was work done at great cost in the clean-up of the Thames and in energy conversion from coal. That kind of experience must have been repeated over and over again and ought to be remembered by all of us. There are no absolutes. If we take a single-minded approach to any policy, then we only damage ourselves. There has to be a balance. In the balance, all of the important elements have to be considered. Certainly one of those, in terms of industrial development, has to be the investment in the environment, which is particularly important to Canada.
How does one invest in the environment? I see nothing wrong with grants being made to corporations that employ Canadians. Grants would allow plants to convert. I see nothing wrong with that. That is being done. I see nothing wrong with our policy of research and development as we try to move to
1.5	per cent of our Gross National Product. Part of that percentage concerns pollution control in the industrial setting. I see nothing wrong with an examination of the tax system in order to determine if tax credits can be used for the purchase and installation of environmental control machinery.
I think we must recognize that there are a number of levels of Government in this country which should be concerned with the environment, whether in the Niagara or the St. Lawrence River area where I grew up and have my home. If there is one fault with the national life in Canada, it is that there has not been sufficient co-operation between many levels of responsible Governments. I think that Canadians have paid a price for the breakdown in federal-provincial relations. We have paid that
Supply
price in the environment, in terms of unemployment and with respect to a whole host of good programs. We have wasted time and energy as a result of bickering between levels of Government.
I suggest that there is a place for Government co-operation in matters concerning the environment, as there is in many other areas. I would like to give the Minister a specific example. I discussed this with him in Brockville. The City of Brockville is situated on the banks of the St. Lawrence. I live beside that river whenever I can in the summer. I grew up there and watched it grow. No one can live beside a river like that and not have it become a part of you to appreciate. The City of Brockville, a progressive city in eastern Ontario, has decided to install a landfill site for municipal garbage on land that abuts on the river. This is a convenient site for the city since it happens to be in the township of Augusta. Therefore, it does not have to put the garbage dump in its own municipality. If this site were situated anywhere else, I believe that the federal Government would not have any jurisdiction at all. However, due to the possible leaching problems from the landfill site into the river, there is a place in that apparatus for more than just consultation. While consultation is important, if there is an environmental assessment hearing about this dump because of its involvement with the St. Lawrence, it gives the federal Government the opportunity to move in and prevent its establishment.
That was the case I wanted to raise with the Minister. I will give him more particulars, if he wishes, because it is important that we stop projects such as these before they begin. I would ask him to go to the Minister of the Environment in Ontario to discuss this issue since a river is involved.
This issue has created some problems in the area. We have had problems with the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes system in any event.
I want to deal with another area in which co-operation is important. The Minister will recall that his Department had suggested that a study be conducted to determine where a new site might be placed in the National Capital area for the disposal of toxic waste from federal Government installations. There were four or five sites set out. Unfortunately, this matter was handled improperly. The public relations for this proposal were very bad and, as a result, I should think that it has been abandoned. I believe it is right that it should be abandoned. As the Hon. Member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis) said, the approach to these matters is extremely important.
However, the problem is still there. The public servants who work in the laboratories and those who live in the surrounding communities are still subject to the improper storage of that chemical waste. I believe if this problem is to be solved it will require co-operation between the federal, provincial and municipal Governments in this part of Ontario if something is to be done here. For instance, at one time there was a proposal by the provincial Government for a central development for the purposes of the storage of those chemical wastes. I believe that is a proper approach to take. I do not see the logic of the
22300

January 27, 1983
Supply
federal Government building one site, the provincial Government building one site, and other companies perhaps having their own sites. All levels should be involved in that area.
My final point once again concerns the United States. We live beside the United States and we have to live together. The good Lord put us on the northern half of the western hemisphere, and we have to learn to live together. I believe that as much support as possible from all sides of the House of Commons should be given to such organizations as the International Joint Commission. The Hon. Member for Niagara Falls is right. The appointment of the Canadian joint Chairman was good. If I were in a position to find someone to qualify for that position, I could find no one more qualified than the appointment that was made. I believe that we have a good combination in Mr. Seaborn and our group on the Commission being coupled with the Hon. Robert McEwen of the United States who lives on the banks of the St. Lawrence outside of Ogdensburg, New York and who feels exactly the same as I do about the importance of the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence waterway and who is prepared to make some noise about the progress in cleaning up the environment.
I would like to suggest to the Minister that he consult with the Chairman of the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission to see if we cannot raise the consciousness of Members of the House of Commons in regard to the importance of that tributary.
I realize that the Minister wrote to various caucus groups and did not receive a great response. Perhaps the reason is that all Members of Parliament are involved. I am talking about Members of Parliament and Senators who represent constituencies contiguous to the river on the Canadian side, and Congressmen and Senators who are interested in the development and preservation of the river and lakes system on the American side. They can become familiar with and express their views on the problems facing both sides in terms of the water quality agreement, the environmental problems, as well as the financial problems on both sides.
I have found that the use of the Canadian-United States interparliamentary group has meant the exchange of ideas and the development of understanding. It is a slow process but one that ought not to be abandoned or discarded merely because it is slow. It is a good process. There will be Governments come and gone. Members of Parliament come and gone, but we can build up an expertise, an understanding and a commitment to cleaning the environment, not only with the Minister but with many Members of the House of Commons.
I have not used all my time but there are other Members who wish to speak. I feel very privileged to have taken part in this debate today, and I want to thank the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) for putting this motion forward so we may deal with a subject that is quite often neglected in the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Mr. Denis Ethier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRON MENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to compliment the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) for introducing this motion and giving us an opportunity to debate this very serious
and complex problem that toxic and hazardous wastes disposal sites cause if not adequately stored or disposed of in safe and guaranteed leak-proof underground sites. This seems to be the case at the dumpsite upstream from Niagara Falls. I compliment the Member for introducing this motion.

However, that is as far as I am prepared to go in the way of compliments, and I may even be tempted to withdraw this one, having listened very carefully to the statements made by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton).

Honestly, I have never heard so many erroneous statements and scare tactics in one single speech. Granted, an Hon. Member during his intervention may commit one or two errors in stating his case, but to carry on during his whole presentation, with false accusations and erroneous statements is not what is expected of an hon. gentleman in this House. Public debate is most welcome and healthy, but one should not use exaggeration in making one's case.
I want to compliment the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I think he was very positive in the suggestion which he brought forth.
The Niagara River Basin and its importance to the Canadian economy and people have been long recognized by the Government. This 37 mile-long river passes through an industrial complex of steel, petrochemical and chemical manufacturing industries which have been the economic lifeblood of this area for the past 30 years. The river itself has provided these industries with a cheap and easy source of hydroelectric power. It has been used by them, in return, as a sewer for their chemical waste.
In the early 1940s, we thought we could have it all and still use the river as a source of drinking water. The Niagara River soon became taxed beyond its limits. We began to see the gross earlier signs of pollution. Those were related to bacterial contamination and were obvious to the eyes and nose. I am speaking of oil slicks, foam, scums and persistent unpleasant odours, as well as visible discoloration of the water. These, the more obvious and crude types of pollution, were, in retrospect, relatively easy to rectify. Limits were placed on discharges of phosphorous and conventional pollutants which quickly removed these signs of pollution. However, within a very short period, more insidious types of chemical pollution began to come to life. They were not visible or easy to identify, but they were there all the same.
The discovery of dioxin by our environmental scientists was the key to the heightened awareness of the extreme danger of these chemicals in the river. In addition, the problem was compounded by the revelation that the major source of the dioxin was the many landfill sites in Niagara Falls, New York. Since dioxin was just one of the many chemicals deposited over the years on these landfill sites, the identification of the
January 27, 1983

problem and the solution became complicated beyond our expectations.
The monitoring of toxic chemicals such as dioxin through the Great Lakes Surveillance Program has led to a more intensive investigation of toxic chemical sources of the Niagara River. Dioxin is a primary example of the legacy which has fallen to us through inadequate control of toxic chemical waste in the past. There is no known source of dioxin currently coming into the Great Lakes Basin. It is the disposal of trichlorophenol waste in landfill sites created in the 1940s and the active dumping of this waste through the 50s, 60s, and up to 1974, which is the suspected cause of extremely high levels of hazardous chemicals now being found.
The first site to come to public attention was the now infamous Love Canal in Niagara Falls, New York. We all know the tragic series of events which eventually led to the full scale investigation of that site. In fact, Love Canal is only one of 215 such sites identified in the American counties of Erie and Niagara Falls. In the case of Love Canal, the Hooker Chemical and Plastics Corporation, now called Occidental Chemical Corporation, had (lumped tons of toxic chemicals in a trench close to a residential neighbourhood. The first shockwaves emanating from Love Canal centred around the health of residents. Our Government quickly became aware of the possibility that chemicals from that site might be leaching into the Niagara River, thereby endangering the health of the Canadian public and environment.
Investigations on Cayuga Creek and Black Creek, which enter the Niagara River from the U.S. side, have shown great cause for concern since high levels of leachate from the Love Canal landfill site are evident in the sediment and fish from these Niagara River tributaries. We are presently investigating the extent of the contamination of these tributaries to identify all the pathways of movement of contaminants from the Love Canal into the Niagara River Basin in order to advise U.S. authorities as to what will constitute, in our opinion, an effective clean-up program.
In fact, the largest landfill site in Niagara Fall, New York, is the Hyde Park site, another Hooker site which, up until 1973, was an open lagoon containing a toxic brew which spilled down Bloody Run Creek directly into Niagara Gorge. Hyde Park landfill site is known to contain up to two and a half tons of TCDD-dioxin-alone and has been the subject of intensive investigation by the Government.
These investigations point to the movement of contaminants into the deep bedrock beneath the landfill and the leaching of toxic waste onto the face of the Niagara Gorge and into the Niagara River. This information was provided to public interest groups in Canada, which, together with their counterparts in the United States, presented oral testimony to the U.S. District Court of New York which is charged with resolving the fate of this site. At the same time, our Government was making active representations to the United States Government for a speedy and complete clean-up of this site, citing international obligations under the Boundary Waters Treaty
Supply
Act of 1909 and the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement of 1972.
I would like to point out that all actions on landfill sites on the Niagara River have occurred during the past several years. Investigation of these sites by the U.S. and Canadian authorities is still under way. It is essential that a complete information base be established before we can determine what cleanup technology would be effective and would prevent these chemicals from entering the environment in the future.
The most recent landfill site we have investigated is the S-Area site, situated just 200 yards from the bank of the Niagara River and constructed on land reclaimed from river waters some years ago. Our preliminary investigation has shown this to be the most serious direct source of contaminants moving from the landfill site into the Niagara River to date. As the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) announced on Monday, portions of landfill containing toxic waste seem to be moving directly into the river and onto Canadian territory. This is the most serious direct example of transboundary chemical pollution we have yet encountered on this river.
In order to determine whether the chemicals from this site are actually on Canadian territory, we will be conducting a further investigation in early spring. At the same time, we are intensifying our efforts to identify chemicals from the S-Area site in fish sediment and water taken from the river. The Department of National Health and Welfare will be testing drinking water on the Canadian side of the Niagara River for these chemicals.
The S-Area landfill has been the subject of intensive consultation with U.S. authorities. Several meetings between the four Governments involved have been held since the summer to present Canadian concerns over the migration of plumes of contaminants moving into and under the Niagara River and the potential hazards created by them. It is our position that the movement of contaminants is not yet well enough defined to determine what remedial technology should be used to either contain or remove the site as a source of contamination to the environment. After our study of S-Area, we will be continuing our investigation with Hooker Site 102nd Street. This particular landfill is situated directly on the bank of the Niagara River and contains toxic waste similar to that deposited in the other three landfills we have previously considered.
We have begun to negotiate with the United States with regard to the release of all confidential data pertaining to this site before the United States court. Action is actively under way. This will enable us to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the dangers of this site and its effect on the Niagara River.
Another major concern on the Niagara River is the continued toxic waste effluent coming from the Niagara Falls, New York, sewage treatment plant. This discharge presently provides a major loading of toxic chemical waste to the Niagara River from the chemical industries in the area. This

January 27, 1983
Supply
treatment plant, originally designed to process and remove highly contaminated chemical wastes, broke down shortly after it was inaugurated and has been in a state of disrepair for the last three years. This means that chemical waste receives only primary treatment and is contributing to the toxic chemical loading of the Niagara River. Numerous diplomatic and technical moves, including direct sampling by Canadians of the effluent from this plant, have been undertaken to press the United States for speedy and effective repairs.
1 would like to emphasize that the toxic chemical pollution of the Niagara River is not a simple problem to describe, let alone solve. 1 have mentioned past discharges from industries which are further compounded by inadequate treatment. These vast landfills, which amount to over a quarter million tons of toxic waste, contain chemicals the identity of which we have yet to discover, and additional new chemicals produced by compounded reaction to each other.
It is a long journey down a dark and twisting path with very few guideposts along the way. Our approach has been to recognize the problem in its entirety while methodically investigating and dealing with the problems on a case-by-case basis. Our progress has been steady and sure, but the complete understanding of these problems lies in the future, as does their resolution.
The excellence of our scientists and engineers provided us with information on which to base our negotiations with the United States. We will use all methods at our disposal to continue to press Canada's case for a complete clean-up of these sources of toxic chemicals to the river.

I would now like to say just a few words about a new phenomenon-I would call it chemophobia-and I am referring to these warnings we are getting practically every week that some new chemical product is hazardous to our health. Far be it from me to criticize the public and the media for getting worried about every new crisis or new discovery that crops up, but I think there is a tendency to make things seem worse than they actually are. I would even go so far as to say that sometimes the facts are concealed to make a better story.
The Government is taking action and is trying to correct the situation. Some Hon. Members may be aware of the program that has been established under the Environmental Contaminants Act. The Department of the Environment and the Department of National Health and Welfare are responsible for evaluating and rating certain industrial chemicals. Unfortunately, not many products have been evaluated, but the Department is now extending its activities to a far greater number of chemical products and by-products. To co-ordinate and integrate all these activities, the Department of the Environment has created the Toxic Chemicals Management Centre. People working at the Centre are responsible for collecting all available data on chemical products and their effects, and for subsequently recommending appropriate action. As these people increase their knowledge of substances
used in industry, the effluent content, the impact of chemical products that have already entered the environment on humans, animals, birds, fish, air, water and soil-as these people get a better picture of the general situation, they can then zero in on certain specific situations. For instance, in factories A, B and C, we have to watch out for chemical product X, or we should give factory D a warning about its disposal methods, or product X is more hazardous than we thought and its use should therefore be prohibited, and so on. Of course all this is not going to be done behind closed doors. The priorities of the Toxic Chemicals Management Program must be open, to scrutiny by industry and other interested parties and the public. That is how the Department will be able to establish a certain level of credibility. It will not necessarily eliminate our chemophobia, but it may help to make us less alarmist.
Finally, a few words about our environmental legislation as it relates to the use of chemical pollutants. The three most important statutes that are concerned with toxic chemicals are: the Environmental Contaminants Act, the Clean Air Act and sections of the Fisheries Act relating to pollution control. This legislation was entirely adequate at the time it was passed, but that is no longer the case, in view of the challenges 1 mentioned earlier. We must therefore prepare new legislation on environmental protection.
I shall give a few examples of various areas that require our attention. The OECD has published international guidelines on laboratory testing of new chemicals. These guidelines have now been approved and we shall therefore have to apply them.
I am aware that the United States has decided to reverse its initial position and now relies on the good faith of the parties concerned with respect to product testing. I am sorry that our main trading partner made this decision, but on the other hand, I am very pleased to note that practically all other member countries in the OECD intend to make these tests compulsory. The new system has a tremendous advantage in that we will be able to obtain far more information and greater reliability.
However, the OECD program applies only to new chemicals. What about the tens of thousands of chemicals that already exist? I know that many products have been tested to some degree, and that a few have been tested quite exhaustively. However, this is only the tip of the iceberg. What are we going to do about the vast number of substances about which we know very little? We shall have to be pragmatic and set our priorities.
As soon as Parliament passes new legislation, we shall make sure that the main responsibility for testing will lie with industry. Other changes will have to be made as well. For instance, our present legislation on water pollution is aimed at protecting fish and not humans. We have to do something about this. The public wants increased protection, and we shall have to act accordingly. I firmly believe that it makes sense to have a comprehensive system for the management of toxical

January 27, 1983

chemicals. Moreover, if we want to maintain our credibility with the public, we shall have to act quickly. I am convinced that we can make chemicals work for us, and that we will succeed.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, once more, I want to ask my hon. colleagues who are going to take part in this debate to refrain from scare tactics when the subject is environmental protection. We often get carried away in the heat of the debate in our statements about the hazards caused by certain industries, without first having checked the extent of the damage that can be caused by such pollutants or toxic chemicals.
I heard the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) who put the motion and who almost scared the people who live in the Niagara Falls area out of their wits when he said that in water, dioxin was an extremely dangerous chemical. We know that. Everybody in Canada does. But to what extent-

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a brief intervention in the 20 minutes I have on the NDP Opposition motion moved by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), which reads as follows:
That this House condemns the Government for its failure to adequately protect the Canadian environment from toxic and hazardous waste and for its subservience to the vested interests of the chemical and industrial waste producers and, in particular, for its failure to expedite the clean-up of the Great Lakes.
Each year, Mr. Speaker, Canadian industries produce approximately one million tonnes of hazardous waste material, and this causes some very serious problems for our society in terms of its effect on our environment, our wildlife, and on the human beings who have to live next to some of the dump sites, or some of the illegal dumps where these hazardous waste materials have been disposed of over the years.
In the past, it was always thought that one of the best ways to protect the environment was to not supersaturate the environment with an excessive amount of pollutants and eventually nature would take care of itself. However, as chemicals have become more complex, research has become more complex and we understand the problems of hazardous waste a bit better, we find that some of the chemicals today, like dioxin in the Great Lakes, have produced some very, very serious problems. Dioxin is not biodegradable and when it is pumped into a natural system, nature itself cannot take care of the pollution which occurs. In Canada there are several dumping sites, almost all of which are totally inadequate for dumping hazardous waste. As a result, we find there has been

dumping into the Niagara River system, and into the Great Lakes. In fact, there is a great amount of dumping which ends up in the Great Lakes.
In the beginning, to be fair to those who dumped the waste many years ago, I suppose they did not know any better. They did not know what the long-term effects of some of these dumping of hazardous and toxic waste could be to our environment. But in this day and age, with our expertise and our research, we know there can be very detrimental effects upon our entire environment. We should be building effective repositories for these waste materials which are harming our society so very much.
I am very concerned about the transportation of hazardous wastes also. The problem of transporting this material through densely populated areas by rail or tanker trucks has caused some very anxious moments to people throughout recent history in Canada where there have been accidents. In fact, life and environment have become endangered. I know that the Department of Transport is looking at this problem now. They have looked at it in the past. I suggest they come up with a few more constructive ideas in terms of transportation of hazardous waste. I know, for example, that no one from the federal Government has been in very close contact with volunteer firefighters, for example, who sometimes find themselves coming into contact with hazardous material and have no knowledge of how to cope with it. I would encourage the federal Government to look at some kind of information program for the Volunteer Firefighting Association across Canada. The volunteer firefighters have to contend with these problems sometimes and they should know exactly what they are dealing with and how they can deal with it.
Dioxin, as I mentioned, is not bio-degradeable. One very small drop in a pitcher of drinking water could cause the death of an entire family if they were to drink that water. These are very dangerous chemicals, indeed. The waste disposal, as I have already said, is inadequate, and we should be addressing this problem very seriously so the waste can be treated, if it needs to be treated, before it gets out into our environment. Certainly the best way to take care of this problem is not to be cleaning up after the fact, but to prevent the pollution problem to begin with. In terms of the cost of cleaning up, I think that the "dumpers", if they do it intentionally and illegally against the wishes of the Government and the people of Canada, should be responsible, and in the case of illegal dumping, should have total responsibility. They should clean up the waste after it has been dumped. Either they should be required to hold insurance, or else there should be some kind of a holdback program on the profits of those companies by the federal Government. When a contractor builds a complex for the Government, whether federal or provincial, there is usually a holdback of 10 per cent, and sometimes 15 per cent, until the building is actually erected and found to be in sound and safe condition. Then the rest of the money is turned over. I submit that a possible way of dealing with those who dump hazardous waste could be that, at the end of the year when their profits are tabulated, their profits could be held back by the federal Government until they act in a responsible manner. If they act in a responsible manner and if there is no unsafe dumping of
hazardous material, then the profits can go back to the company. That should be coupled with insurance. I think there should be great emphasis put on these people so that they do not abuse the very privileged position which some of them hold.
I would like to move to a few local concerns. I am very concerned about the problem of acid rain, which is not only a Canadian problem, it is an international problem, because of the very fact that the pollutants get into the atmosphere, the sulphates and nitrates which cause acid precipitation, and they come down with no recognition of international boundaries.
Environment Canada, I know, has a testing station at Cree Lake, in the riding which 1 represent. They are monitoring very closely the amount of acid precipitation in that area of Saskatchewan which, incidentally is just on the edge of the Cambrian Shield in the northern part of my home province. Acid rain could become a very serious problem in Western Canada. I hope it never gets to the point at which we have seen it affect the Province of Ontario where there are hundreds and hundreds of lakes which are dead. They support no life in terms of organic material, fish, or insects which used to be around those lakes. They support no life, and I would not want it to move any further than it has already.
Another situation I would like to talk about, Mr. Speaker, is that which occurred on January 24, the Government of Canada, DREE and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce announced an incentive of some $74,000 plus to Canadian Seed Coaters Limited of Brampton, Ontario who indicated a desire to open a new facility for the processing of canola, or rapeseed as it is traditionally known, in the Batt-lefords area. The total project will cost some $215,000 and provide seven new jobs. I commend this company for moving into the Battlefords area. I think it is very good to see them recognize the benefits derived from being located in northwestern Saskatchewan. I also welcome the jobs provided in a time of rising unemployment because there is a great need for more jobs throughout Canada. I am also pleased to see that the farmers of that area, who buy treated rapeseed, will now be able to buy it from a local processor. I have some concern, however, about this company and its activities. I would like to put those on the record since they have a direct connection with the motion put forward today by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton).
That company is going to be using a chemical called Lindane in the treatment of the canola. There is not much information around as to how they are going to use this chemical or bring it into the Battlefords area, so I would like to say a few words about Lindane itself. The process to be used in the plant is twofold. One, they use Vitavax rs Flowable which provides the canola seed with a coating of protection from the Flea beetle and fungal diseases which attack the seed once it is in the ground. I am thinking of Blackleg which is a problem there
January 27, 1983

right now. They are also using what is called super phosphates as a fertilizer and they will also coat the seed with that. I want to put on the record that we should be watching very carefully the Vitavax rs Flowable process. Vitavax is made up of three chemicals: Carbathiin and Thiram, which prevent fungal diseases from growing on the plant. The other chemical, the one I am more concerned about, is Lindane. As far as Lindane is concerned, the United States Environmental Protection Agency, in June of 1980, recommended banning its use. I quote:
After careful consideration the agency has concluded that the risks of use on these crops, even reduced by protective measures, outweigh the benefits of use in so far as the benefits are presently known and therefore recommends cancellation.
I guess what they are saying is that the detrimental effect of the use of Lindane can quite well outweigh its benefits. Now I am not supporting or denying that statement, but I want to put on record the very serious concern some people have expressed regarding Lindane. Many people who advocate its use say that it is a very dangerous chemical, but what are the alternatives to not using it? They maintain that careful use of Lindane can be an asset to those in the agricultural sector when it is used for coating canola seed. However, there are problems with humans when it comes to the use of Lindane. The EPA says that exposure to Lindane in humans can cause symptoms of acute poisoning. Therefore, the people who are going to be using this chemical want to know what is going to be done to protect them from exposure to Lindane in the plant where the seeds are going to be treated. The symptoms of this acute poisoning appear in a kind of chronological order. First, there is dizziness, headaches; nausea and vomitting set in, which can be followed by diarrhea, tremors, a noticeable weakness, convulsions, heart problems, eventually a bluish tinge to the complexion and some kind of eventual circulatory collapse. The EPA is also particularly concerned that this chemical produces acute effects in children even more significant than it produces in adults. The EPA produced a report, and Agriculture Canada circulated a report from the Winnipeg Free Press which said:
The report also cited the case of a two and a half month old infant who died after being treated for scabies with a lindane product. A concentration of 110 parts per billion of lindane in the child's brain was considered the most probable cause of death.
Lindane is also used in other products such as flea soap for pets, and we should be very careful of this product because of its very dangerous effects. Workers who must be exposed to Lindane, Mr. Speaker, are advised to wear long-sleeved shirts and pants and some kind of protective clothing to avoid exposure of the arms and legs to this chemical. They should wear gloves to prevent exposure to their hands, and to a degree some protection of the face. It is also very important that they wear disposable masks or masks of some kind, so that they cannot inhale dust particles or fumes from the Lindane. I would like to see the new company moving into the Battlefords make sure that it observes these very simple measures of protection for its workers.

As to not following a proper procedure, Mr. Speaker, there was a case of a farmer dying in Manitoba. A Mr. Kerr, who farmed near Cardale, some 50 kilometres northeast of Brandon, died of kidney failure last spring, nine days after he was admitted to hospital with symptoms of chemical poisoning. This man had stirred some Vitavax with his arm in a tub, and of course the chemical entered through the pores of his skin and that was the eventual cause of his death.
Lindane has been used extensively in Saskatchewan. The 1978-79 report of the Saskatchewan Environmental Advisory Council said that Lindane was widespread in rivers, lakes and other surface water in the Province, particularly in the Qu'Appelle River district. Bottom sediments, where agricultural chemicals accumulate and serve as a sink for toxic substances, pose not just an immediate but also a long-term potential threat to the environment. Lindane is among the more than 100 chemicals involved in fraudulent and inadequate safety tests carried out by industrial biotest laboratories in the United States in the late 1970s. Right now Lindane is one of the chemicals being re-evaluated by the Department of National Health and Welfare, but the results of those tests are not known yet. I urge that those results become known very quickly, and if there is any alternative to the chemical Lindane in the seed-coating process, I would like to see Agriculture Canada recommend it to anyone who wants to go into the business of coating seeds.
According to Steven Safe, a biochemist at Guelph University and an expert on toxicity, Lindane is slow to degrade and can accumulate in human fat cells. If one is exposed to it over a long period of time, the chemical can accumulate in the body and cause some of the side effects I have referred to. He has said that the problem with widespread use is that when Lindane gets into the water system, it can get into other organisms. It is very important to keep Lindane from getting into our food chain as it is so very detrimental to health.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like it on the record that I want to know from the company that will build the seed coating plant in the Battlefords, what it is going to do to provide safe working conditions for the people who work there. I think it should provide adequate information to those farmers who buy their product so that they do not handle it in a way that may be dangerous. I understand that there will be very little chemical waste from the plant, but I should like to know their plans to dispose of what waste there is.
I have welcomed the company into the Battleford area, Mr. Speaker. If it acts as a responsible citizen in the community, providing jobs and services, then as the local Member of Parliament I will be a friend and supporter of the company. On the other hand, if the company acts irresponsibly, as many others have been allowed to, I will be a thorn in its side for as long as it remains in the Battlefords.
