There are eight questions on record, Mr. Speaker, rather than just one, and none about the raccoon dog. We did not even find that one. I hope the Hon. Member for Skeena is sorry that he gave misleading information to the House.
I would now like to deal with one or two matters, but I shall not take too long with them because I know a lot of other Members want to speak in this debate.
I commend the Hon. Member for bringing the motion forward. The protection of the Canadian environment, and the provisions of clean air and good water is everyone's business. Too often we think that these matters are only the business of Government. Certainly Government has a responsibility for the environment. In Alberta there is a Clean Air and Clean Water Act, and I believe most other Provinces have something similar. It is important to set standards that everyone can follow.
I should like to deal with the matter of good water in the Canadian environment, and I will refer to a rather different type of poison from those we have heard about today and that is, parasite poisoning.
Giardia lamblia organisms exist in two forms, as a living parasite and as a cyst. Only the cyst form is infectious to man, however, since the living parasite is destroyed in the digestive process. The Alberta provincial laboratories personnel who provide Parks Canada with testing services, discovered the giardia cyst. The gardia lamblia parasite causes vomiting, stomach flu, and sometimes, paralysis. Once it occurs in an area it continues to be a problem. It can be caused by poor handling of food anywhere in Canada. Probably the most common form is that it comes in the form of cysts from beavers. That is where the colloquial name has come from, "beaver fever". This cyst has got into the water supply in the townsite of Banff, and of course once it is in there it is very difficult to deal with.
The matter was reported to the Hon. Minister of the Environment, and the Minister decided he would have a study made in regard to this, which he did. He appointed a very excellent firm of consulting engineers, the Stanley Associates Engineering Ltd., and a very excellent report came out. The report indicated that the Banff water system has no facilities except chlorination to control giardia lamblia cysts, and chlorination becomes less effective at temperatures below 5 degrees Centigrade. It is worse in the winter months, and this is now the second year, when this has caused concern and sickness, and it is a very worrying thing. If notices continue to be handed to everybody who goes into the park and notices are posted in all public places not to drink the water, it is going to have the effect of keeping people away from that beautiful tourist area, which has taken years to develop and is now a world renowned area. People will not go to places if they are going to get sick while they are there.

Any consideration of water must also take into account the population which the system will serve. At the present time the Banff townsite has a population of probably 17,000, and the engineering firm said that by the year 2005 the population will be 35,000. That includes a reasonable amount of the one million people who travel through there, mostly in the summer months.
In view of the water projected demands, as the report indicates, the need for expansion of the water system is evident. I am not going to deal with that aspect today, but I am going to deal with this matter of the cysts that are in the water, and urge the Department to take a very definite stand in putting in an effective water filtration system.
Normally, in the Province of Alberta, if water does not reach a certain standard, the municipality is required by law to put in a water treatment system. Banff, of course, being under the control of the federal Government, does not come under the provincial regulations. If Banff was a normal town in Alberta, the town would have been ordered to find the money and put in a water treatment system, because it is essential that every municipality and every Government is careful to make sure we have good drinking water. Infected water is what is worrying the people of Banff today.
The importance of putting in a water treatment system has received a great deal of study. It is an expensive process. The engineers have come up with a suggestion that $10.2 million would provide a system that not only provides water that meets all the qualities of good drinking water but provides a water treatment system that would serve the people for many, many years. I think this is essential. When we say $10.2 million, it certainly sounds like a lot of money, but we have to remember that the federal Government has, in the last full fiscal year, collected more than $6.5 million from the Banff area, and that has been going on for many years because a million or more people go there, from all parts of the world, every year.
I think it is essential that we stop trying to use palliatives or bandaids in this particular area and face the issue and put in a water treatment system. That is the only cure. Medical people tell me there is no other way of effectively destroying the cysts and stopping the spread of this disease. What I hope never happens is that someone will die from this disease, and that is quite possible. I have a stack of letters from people who have become sick, very, very ill, from the water. Water was the common cause, the health unit doctor tells me. So it is essential that we get a water treatment system in Banff at the earliest possible time.
I strongly recommend to the Minister and the officials of Parks Canada that the recommendations of Stanley Associates Engineering be followed and acted on immediately. It is over a year since this has become a problem, and surely we should put our money where our mouth is and make sure that the people in that area have good, clean drinking water. That is an important part of our environment.
I think that any national park within a Province should come under the rules and regulations of the standards set by

that Province in regard to clean air and clean water. I think the national parks, because they are a separate entity, should not be excused from the standards that have been set by the provincial Governments. Certainly a number of people are concerned about it.
I want to give just one or two indications of how widespread the concern is. In the Banff School District, the Chairman of the Banff Community School Committee, which is an elected body, wrote to the Hon. Minister on June 21, 1982. It reads:
It has come to our attention that Parks Canada has not yet made a decision whether to install a water treatment plant in Banff, therefore we would like to strongly recommend that Parks Canada take immediate action to have such a plant built.
The problem of giardia lambia in the Banff water system still persists and it is a severe health hazard to the residents of Banff. In addition, one must consider the millions of tourists who visit the town annually and have no facilities with which to boil water to ensure that it is fit for consumption.
That is from local people.
Then we had a letter from a medical doctor from Quebec from the Laurenval School Board which reads:
I have just returned from a two week conference with the Canadian Education Association at Banff, Alberta.
He goes on to say:
The presence of giardiasis in the Banff water supply is a potentially dangerous situation with long-term ill effects possible.
This is from a medical doctor from Quebec who is very concerned that no action is being taken about this, and it is a serious matter. An ordinary, everyday citizen wrote that she suffered a great deal of illness, and she wonders why we are finding new wells and then putting that water into the water system that already has cysts in it. We could go on and on. I do not want to take the time of the House with regard to that but it is not just simply the local people who have complaints. It is people who are highly trained and people who realize what this giardis lambia can do to the human body. What the long term effects of it are is still something which is even more questionable.
The Department now has the set-up, and I think that Parks Canada will make a very serious mistake if they now start to try to bandaid this problem by digging new wells and doing this and that and the other thing. It will never be cheaper than it is right now to put in a water treatment system. A water treatment system is going to be required eventually, and it will never be cheaper than right now. I strongly urge the Department to give this serious consideration and to not let this situation continue.
I have one other letter from a medical doctor from Ontario who is very concerned about this. He wrote his own Member and said:

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 62-PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRON MENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I do not agree with the tone and the detail of the resolution today, I welcome the chance to speak in this debate. I would certainly not be telling you anything new or startling if I were to say that the public perception of the chemical industry these days is not a very flattering one. In fact, this was the subject of an article on the editor's page of a recent issue of Chemical and Engineering News. The title of the article was "Chemophobia," that is, fear of chemicals. It was about a phenomenon so widespread that this term has been coined to characterize it. It is interesting that we seem to like to put things into context and perhaps change our language in order to make something more relevant. Chemophobia reminds me of a story that I read. Unfortunately, I cannot remember who the author was, but he wrote: "We no longer live in the slums. We live in the inner city." He wrote, "Once I was poor and then I was needy. Next I was deprived, and the last thing 1 knew I was disadvantaged. I still did not have a nickel to my name, but I sure had a great vocabulary." We can add chemophobia to our vocabulary.
It is one of the ironies of our society that we demand the standard of living that chemicals, among other things, have given us, and we are unwilling to see that standard decline. Yet, at the same time, we seem reluctant to pay the full price that the safe use of chemicals demands. The thrust of the
January 27, 1983

article was that chemophobia has reached such proportions that the chemical industry has been, to a certain extent, paralyzed by it, and is on the defensive as a result.
A good part of the public's wariness stems from the sheer intimidation that a layman feels when confronted by a seemingly impenetrable mass of scientific jargon, more of the so-called Newspeak like chemophobia. This, and the fact that chemicals are all around us and not necessarily to be feared, was neatly brought home in an article run in a quality periodical. 1 believe it was the New Yorker. The ad simply consisted of an attractive and appetizing picture of a "natural" orange. Appended to this was a list of the chemicals it contained, which was as long as your arm.
I think it was the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) who discussed a problem which was very complicated which, in turn, indicated how complex the whole problem is.
I am glad to have an opportunity for a few moments to talk a little bit about the science of toxicology, what a toxicologist does and the role he plays in helping us to solve this most complex problem. Recently I had a chance to read a planning study about the establishment of a Canadian centre for toxicology. This was developed by the University of Guelph and the University of Toronto. While the study talks about centres in Guelph and Toronto, it looks as though this plan could easily be expanded to have national scope. I am very proud of the fact that one of the universities that is involved in this study is the University of Guelph which happens to be my Alma Mater. I think it is important to realize the potentials of an institute such as this and to see how lacking we really are in basic knowledge of many of the problems that are related to toxic substances in our environment. There are other terms which are again part of our Newspeak. We talk about things that are either gross or microscopic and we talked about micro or macro. We have no difficulty with chemicals which appear in such high concentration that they can be tasted and seen. They provide some warning about their presence. The major problem we will face in the future concerns those chemicals that are present in amounts that are infinitesimal. These chemicals only cause problems after they have been consumed constantly in these small amounts.
A fortunate fact to remember is that our environment contains natural sentinels to detect environmental problems. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) talked about the beaver. No doubt, they were finding this illness in beavers. The fact that they found a cyst in the beaver and that the beavers were probably dying gave us some indication that there was a problem. This happens very often in our environment.
I would like to elaborate on the institution of toxicology. The proposal is to create this institution called the Canadian Centre for Toxicology. Although it will draw heavily upon existing strengths in toxicology of the University of Guelph and the University of Toronto, it will be an autonomous
Supply
institution operated in partnership with Governments, industry, labour and universities. I think this is an important consideration. It will have the credibility of an independent organization which adheres to the highest standards of scientific integrity. It will interface with other institutions across Canada to form an integral part of the total network, and will foster a co-operative approach among these organizations.
What will be the intent of this organization? They go on to say in this report that the dangers which the increasing use of toxic chemicals present to human health and the environment are now the subject of acute and valid public concern. They go on to say that these concerns arise because we do not know enough about these chemicals to weigh their long-term effects. The public does not believe that existing regulations provide adequate protection, and they demand more assurance. In some instances, the public in pressing for action, has been ill-informed but it is clear that some toxins do pose risks to human health and to the environment. The extent of these risks is poorly understood.
This new institute for toxicology wants to see major new efforts being made to obtain data on these compounds to regulate them wisely and therefore be able to reduce the risk of their use. Incidents of damage will continue to occur, and some will be disastrous, but unless such incidents are prevented, extensive and costly corrective action will be needed. We are seeing evidence of this today, costly, corrective, after-the-fact solutions.
Another danger we have is that public pressure might force unwarranted removal of important chemicals from the market and place our resource and secondary industries at a competitive disadvantage. I find the description in this proposal about the statement of need and intent to be very relevant to the debate today.
Another area in which we are deficient in Canada is research. I would like to talk for a moment about research in toxicology and what that means. First, what is a toxicologist? A toxicologist is a scientist in his or her own right. It is the science that deals with the effects of poisons on living organisms, from micro-organisms to man. It also deals with the effects on the entire living systems, a type of ecotoxicology. As well, toxicology increasingly deals with controlling, curing and avoiding the harmful effects of toxic chemicals on life.
Toxicology must determine the impact of toxic substances on man and his environment so that decisions can be made on the use of toxicants based on a valid system of risks and benefits.
I hope I have made it quite clear that I am very supportive of this institute of toxicology which these two universities have established and for which they are attempting to receive support.
I would like to close by saying that there are probably fewer than 200 trained toxicologists in Canada. If the science of toxicology is to be pursued, we naturally must train more of these scientists. During the last 30 years, a series of disasters have focused attention on the inadequacy of the science of

January 27, 1983
Supply
toxicology. I do not need to mention thalidomide, methyl mercury, dioxin or PCBs. There is a whole list.
1 would like to draw to your attention the fact that the necessity for training toxicologists, for learning more about these toxic substances and therefore developing a high category of toxicologists in Canada is very important. If for no other reason, I took part in this debate today to bring the importance of this science to the attention of the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped to have a few minutes to participate in this debate. Since there are only approximately two minutes remaining, I would just like to express my dismay and displeasure at the lack of leadership we have had from the Government across the way in environmental problems in the last 15 years. In fact, they have been in Government for the last 20 years, going back to the days of Lester Pearson. We are still polluting our lakes and air and creating an exceedingly unhealthy environment for all Canadians. I suggest that it is a damning indictment of a Government that is more concerned with the profits of its friends in the companies and corporations and with lining the pockets of the rich. I include my friend, the Minister of Agriculture, (Mr. Whelan), who is a born again capitalist like Ronald Reagan, as are the other Ministers in the Cabinet.
It is sad that they make that their priority while letting the environment suffer. The Great Lakes are being polluted and we are producing millions of tons of wastes every year. There are very few controls. The fish are being poisoned.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR BEEF INDUSTRY
AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR BEEF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) a question in the House which reads as follows:
In view of Ihc very depressed situation in the Canadian beef industry this year, with low cattle prices last fall and continuing high input costs for interest and farm machinery repairs, is the Minister planning to implement the provisions of the Anderson-Vandermeulen Report on the beef industry, or provide stabilization payments to producers this winter? What action is planned by the Government?
The Minister went on to say that he was having a series of discussions regarding this matter. I asked the Minister this question because on August 28 of 1981, the Minister of Agriculture announced that he was establishing a commission consisting of Mr. E. H. Anderson and Mr. H. M. Vandermeul-en to report on the state of the beef cattle industry in Canada. The press release indicated the whole range of tremendous problems facing the Canadian Agriculture Industry today, including input costs. In relation to Mr. Anderson and Mr. Vandermeulen, the press release also stated:
They will report to Mr. Whelan by January, 1982, on how the interests of Canadian consumers can be best served in a manner consistent with Canadian economic development while, at the same time, permitting the industry to expand and producers to make a living commensurate with their risk-taking, labour and management ability.
In fact, that report was made just about a year ago.
Mr. Anderson came to my constituency and held meetings with a number of beef producers both on Manitoulin Island and in the District of Algoma. We had a good chance to discuss the very serious problems with a representative group of producers. At that time, interest rates were much higher. The Government has taken some steps relating to reduction in interest rates for farm credit loans. We discussed with that group their interest in stabilization programs and the continuing problem of imports from offshore. Of course, this past fall we had difficulty when the Americans cut off our imports; not of live cattle but, rather, of red meat.
Those producers outlined a complete list of rising input costs, such as fertilizer, machinery and fuel costs, and gave a complete rundown of problems facing their industry. Most of those circumstances have not changed. Now, only a year later, input costs continue to rise. In fact, the returns for beef producers have not increased at all. This past fall, prices for cow-calf operators and general beef producers have continued to be unacceptably low.
Likewise, during our meeting at Algoma, we discussed stabilization and the problem of reconciling Provincial programs. Some of the western Provinces, such as Saskatchewan and Alberta, have extensive stabilization programs for their cow-calf producers. We discussed the control of imports, the cost of interest and money and so on.
I must say that both Mr. Anderson and Mr. Vandermeulen really approached the problem with a very sympathetic ear to the producers. I hope the Minister will be able to make that report public. I know the producers would like to read it. In any event, I hope the Minister and the Government will move
January 27, 1983

very soon on the provisions of that report. Of course, it would be much better if it could be made available to Members of Parliament and the general public in order that they could see those recommendations. I am sure many of them are worthwhile.
The other question I put to the Minister was whether the industry would qualify this year for stabilization payments. Traditionally they had to be stabilized at 90 per cent of the average over the last five years. The Government should move to bring that to at least 100 per cent, and reconcile on a national basis the various provincial programs. Some Provinces have such programs. As far as I know, there is no stabilization program in Ontario this year. I hope the Minister will move on a national program.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE FOR BEEF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to answer the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) concerning the beef industry. Some people may be surprised that the constituency of Algoma has such a large beef industry. I have visited many times with the Hon. Member and I realize the importance the beef industry holds for his constituency.
I want to begin by recalling the conditions in the industry which caused me to ask for the Anderson Vandermeulen Report. We have had several types of reports and studies. I said that we needed somebody to put those together in order to come up with some solutions.
From 1979 to the present, beef producers in Canada have faced the most difficult period since the Second World War. Hog prices as well were low to 1980 and 1981, and began to pick up only in mid-1982. Bankruptcies among beef and hog producers in 1981 were very high; much higher than in 1982. Beef and hog producers in some regions of Canada appear to have been hurt worse than in others. Beef producers in the Grey-Bruce Peninsula of Ontario and parts of the Alberta industry appear to have been suffering the most. The Province of Alberta produces approximately 42 per cent of total beef production in Canada. Flog producers in Quebec have suffered major losses resulting in the first downturn in that industry in Quebec in some years.
I want to recall this, and I am sure the Hon. Member is aware of it. I proposed 100 per cent income insurance to the Provinces in 1978 for all products; beef, pork and all other agricultural products. This was turned down by the Provinces at that time. The same people are now asking me to please come forward with a plan which will stabilize this industry. They do not say, "like the one you proposed in 1978". That is what I proposed then. Even farm organizations turned it down. 1 had Cabinet approval. We then had the Clark Government which took the authority away from its Minister. They queashed the idea, saying it was too costly. Some Members on that side are now asking for that type of plan.
Because of the difficulties faced in this industry I asked Mr. Anderson and Mr. Vandermeulen to explore all its aspects,
Adjournment Debate
every part. As the Hon. Member for Algoma said, some Provinces do not have plans. Some cannot afford one, and some have hit-and-miss programs. They are all saying they want a national plan.
The study included not only an examination of farm-level marketings, but as well the packing, wholesale and distribution of red meats. The report was finalized in 1982, with translations and that type of thing, and it is now before Cabinet. We have had one or two discussions on it, and we hope to finalize them in the next three weeks.
As far as stabilization is concerned, there will be no payment if we just use 90 per cent. If we use 90 per cent of the five-year average, there will be a payment. We have made certain recommendations in accordance with the laws we have to abide by, the Agricultural Stabilization Act, 1975. 1 want a program that will get the most returns from the marketplace and not from the Treasury of the nation.

subtopic: PRIVACY-MISUSE OF PERSONAL INFORMATION STORED IN COMPUTERS
PRIVACY-MISUSE OF PERSONAL INFORMATION STORED IN COMPUTERS
speechtext:
Protection of privacy now lags far behind available computer technology. An unprecedented amount of information about Canadians is now in computer banks and we will see a very dramatic increase in the near future, but we have little or no protection against abuse or misuse of that information.
In answer to my question in the House on January 25, the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan) confirmed that the question of creating a new offence for the misuse of personal information is now under consideration. I would also like to see the Government give some leadership to those in the information industry, encouraging them to draw up voluntary guidelines respecting the use of information in their banks. Some industry spokesmen have said that the only privacy protection they can offer clients is their word, because the potential problems are complex, and they will have to wait for some years to see what the problems really are in order to develop appropriate ways of dealing with them. 1 would prefer to see a serious effort made now to increase confidentiality protection, and to build some measures of protection into new computer programs from the beginning.
Most Canadians welcome the exciting development of new technology which has delivered many new services and greater efficiency in many areas, and has unlimited potential to add to the quality of life. However, each new computerization of data compiled by hand, and each consolidation of information in data banks, spreads personal data further and further afield from the person who has responsibility for it.
Having good medical information in computer banks covering the years of one's life may be of great help if one arrives in a strange hospital and a good history is needed, but there is also potential for embarrassment if, for instance, that information is known and is used to make the case that someone has health problems and is not fit for a job which he or she

January 27, 1983
Adjournment Debate
very badly wants. So at every side there is an advantage and a potential problem.
Many home owners are now using computerized security services; doors and buzzers are wired to a device attached to the cable line and the systems send an electronic alert to the cable company in case of medical emergency, burglary or fire, so that the cable company can phone for ambulance, police or fire brigade, as the case may be. Many of these systems are being purchased by people who are very pleased to have an additional sense of security. In the interest of providing that security, the systems sweep the home at frequent intervals. Information about a family's routines, if it fell into the wrong hands, could in fact be used by the very criminals from whom the system was supposed to protect the home owner. The quickly developing two-way computer system which enables viewers to do credit card shopping, banking and select from electronic newspapers at home has enormous potential value in terms of convenience, particularly for people at home caring for young children or sick relatives, or for handicapped persons. There is potential to enlarge their frontiers enormously. However, information about financial transactions going into the wrong hands could be misused.
I raise this matter not in the interest of being sensational or over-emphasizing the problem, but rather in the interest of promoting reasoned, practical safeguards and solutions now while there still is time and before we are overtaken by events.

speakeroldname: Mr. Al MacBain (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PRIVACY-MISUSE OF PERSONAL INFORMATION STORED IN COMPUTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) raises a very serious matter and there can be no suggestion in my reply that there was any sensationalism either in the presentation or the subject matter she raises.
The Privacy Commissioners' Study was commissioned specifically to obtain guidance on whether the Government should act to regulate the use of the Social Insurance Number in Canada. While Ms. Hansen recommended that there was no need to regulate the use of the Social Insurance Number, she did point out that there was a problem associated with data-linkage, which is part of a more widespread problem concerning the unauthorized use of personal information. This is the very subject addressed by the Hon. Member for Trinity this evening.
The Commissioners' recommendation was that an offence be included in the Criminal Code to prohibit dishonest dealings with personal data provided to obtain a benefit or service, under compulsion of law, or has been placed for private use in the custody of another. The recommendation has significant federal-provincial implications since the area of data protection outside the federally regulated sphere to a great extent involves the Provinces. Although the Provinces have not yet acted in this area, the use of the Criminal Law power by the federal Government to regulate the use and exposure of personal information might, without provincial involvement, be
viewed by them as intruding on some aspect of their responsibility. The Privacy Commissioners' recommendation has been brought to the attention of provincial Governments and their views upon it have been sought. However, because of the nature of the issue, any proposal to act upon it would have to be subject to future consultation.
The proposal to create such a criminal offence is being reviewed as part of the Criminal Law review. Some part of the recommendation, as it relates to computerized personal data, may be incorporated as part of the recommendation regarding computer crime.
We are also looking at the wider issue of the general protection of privacy, more in line with what the Hon. Member was directing us to this evening. In some countries in western Europe this whole protection of computerized data is dealt with in a regulatory scheme. There is built in a process of review by the regulatory body to ensure compliance with the conditions of the licence. That use and disclosure scheme could be similar to the one now presently contained in the new federal Privacy Act.
Is my time up, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SUGGESTED SCHOOL ATTENDANCE FOR RECIPIENTS
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SUGGESTED SCHOOL ATTENDANCE FOR RECIPIENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 8 I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) if he would introduce changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I wanted to see some changes which would allow unemployed workers to improve their job qualifications by attending school while collecting Unemployment Insurance. I asked the question in light of the 1.5 million Canadians unemployed, for whom no jobs exist. The Minister chose to downplay the unemployment crisis in Canada and simply repeated the obvious fact that the Act already had some provisions for training. He did not deal with the fact, which I had mentioned in my question, that there were long waiting lists for UIC sponsored training programs. The Minister's answer did, however, faithfully reflect the policy of his Department and Government. It denied a tragedy taking place in Canadian homes and communities through unemployment, and ignored the possibilities for constructive action which could and should be taken. Many laid-off workers want to use the misfortune of unemployment as an opportunity for further training. Now is the time the Government should take seriously the need for and possibility of improving the skills of Canadian workers. Let me give a couple of examples from my own constituency, even though this is a national problem.
I know a young father, who is very concerned because he is beginning to develop some symptoms of the nervous disease known as "whitehand" which affects workers who have to use
January 27, 1983

vibrating tools such as power saws. He knows he cannot continue as a faller in the woods forever. He would like to use the time when he is laid off to take vocational training. All of the U1C sponsored programs in his area of interest, however, have waiting lists of up to two years. He does not want to waste the time when he is unemployed, but he has no choice. If he goes ahead on his own and enrols in a course, his Unemployment Insurance payments will be cut off. As a married man with a family, he cannot afford that and he worries that a few years ahead whitehand might make it impossible for him to keep his faller's job. This is the time it should be possible for him to take a training program.
Another young man worked at the Chemainus sawmill which was closed indefinitely last year. When he enrolled in a school to train as a mechanic, his Unemployment Insurance payments were cut off. When he appealed, his appeal was denied. I should like to read some excerpts from a letter he wrote which outlines his case. He begins:
I have been unemployed for some months now. I have been cut off of UI because the umpire, board of appeals etc. felt I am some sort of leech. This is not true. I am pursuing diligently even DESPERATELY the difficult task of finding work. I am only running into dead ends everywhere. I will take any job anywhere, anytime, anyplace-
Eventually I want to be a mechanic. The board of review seems to have seized on this to suggest I am picky about the jobs I will take. They say I want more than minimum wage. I ask you, WHO DOESN'T? 1 have worked at less than minimum wage on most of the tasks 1 have found since 1 lost my job.
It is the only work 1 can find. I took the attitude that maybe these small jobs might lead to something better, but unfortunately they did not. They did not last.
1 want a job that is permanent and full time. This is my idea of a job. The board of review seems to think because of this 1 will not take other jobs. This is untrue, my record speaks for itself. A review of my report cards will show I take any job I can get.
I am going to school to try to improve my chances of getting a job. What is wrong with that? I asked manpower to sponsor me but they refused. They said they would add my name to the wait list. There is a four year wait. The course is being cut permanently in about 5 months. So 1 took the course anyway on my own initiative. It is a lot of money but I am desperate for a job and in today's job market it seems my chances are getting worse and worse.
I am an insulted person, if manpower phoned me up and said they had a job for me 1 would not hesitate to take it.
The board of review had some interesting comments on the case. It found him a very direct and forthright youth, and said that they certainly admired his tenacity and ambition.
Surely in this period of unemployment, changes could be made to the Act which would allow unemployed workers
Adjournment Debate
greater scope of education. If they are taking training for jobs and trades in which a skill shortage is likely to occur, they should be allowed to do so while continuing to receive unemployment insurance benefits. We should not see another lost generation ahead of us, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Remi Bujold (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE-SUGGESTED SCHOOL ATTENDANCE FOR RECIPIENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) previously answered part of the Hon. Member's question here in the House. As he pointed out at the time, we do not have to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to enable people receiving benefits to go to school. The Act already contains a provision, namely Section 39, which provides that individuals directed to authorized training courses are eligible for unemployment insurance benefits for the duration of the course and for six additional weeks. These measures are not linked exclusively to the occupational training program since they apply to practically all authorized courses.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, in its expenditures for job creation and training courses for the unemployed, the Goven-ment is not restricted to funds coming out of the Unemployment Insurance account. People who are not eligible for unemployement insurance benefits can receive allowances providing them with some financial assistance while they receive training. Of course, Mr. Speaker, there are long waiting lists. But the House will agree that our most recent legislation on occupational training concentrated on courses that would prepare students for existing jobs. Not long ago, we had a very important conference here in Ottawa to discuss employment opportunities in the years to come, and the possibility of organizing training courses in such a way that the vast majority of unemployed Canadians would be able to receive training in high technology subjects and thus re-enter the labour market.
